articles.title: A Taxonomy of Misleading Mental Health Content Online
articles.authors: Nicole Bizzotto
articles.abstract: Online mental health communication can mislead without containing demonstrably incorrect claims. This article introduces a taxonomy of misleading online mental health content, distinguishing between source-, message-, and decoding-level misleadingness. It provides researchers, clinicians, and online platforms with a framework for identifying potentially harmful mental health content online that veracity-based approaches may overlook.

articles.title: Expertise Diversity Enhances Information Sharing in Wiki settings: Evidence from Sequential Collaboration
articles.authors: Maren Mayer; Joachim Kimmerle
articles.abstract: Online collaborative projects like Wikipedia rely on sequential collaboration, where individual contributors iteratively revise a shared product. While previous research has examined wikis for collaborative writing and sequential collaboration for numerical judgments, little is known about the cognitive mechanisms underlying information sharing in such settings. The present study bridges research on collaborative writing, group information sharing, and cognitive models of sequential collaboration. Drawing on a computational model of sequential collaboration, we tested whether higher variation in contributors’ expertise facilitates the integration of information into a shared text. In an experiment with 413 participants, we demonstrate that information accumulation increased throughout the sequential chain but at a decreasing rate. Consistent with model predictions, higher expertise variation resulted in more information being incorporated into the shared text. Contrary to expectations, expertise variation did not affect the speed of information accumulation, nor did it increase information deletions. These findings demonstrate that predictions derived from a cognitive model of numerical judgment formation generalize to information-sharing contexts. More broadly, the results suggest that diversity in contributors’ knowledge can improve collaborative knowledge construction in sequential environments. This research adds to evidence that sequential collaboration is an effective mechanism for integrating distributed knowledge in online collaborative systems.

articles.title: Infants’ Social Evaluations Revisited: An Updated Meta-Analysis
articles.authors: Francesco Margoni; Alvin Wei Ming Tan
articles.abstract: Over the past twenty years, numerous studies have suggested that infants prefer prosocial agents—who help, comfort, or act fairly—over antisocial agents, who harm others or act unfairly. However, the field has faced replication challenges, including a recent multi-lab failed replication, raising concerns about the robustness of these effects. In response, we updated and extended an earlier meta-analysis, synthesizing 182 effect sizes from published and unpublished studies, with an aggregate sample of 4,089 infants aged 0–32 months, using manual choice and visual preference measures. The estimated meta-analytic raw proportion for infants’ preference for prosocial over antisocial agents was 0.65, 95% CI [0.61, 0.68]. This preference was largely stable across age, type of measure, stimulus format, and scenario type, but there was some evidence that larger studies yielded smaller effects. No clear evidence of publication bias was detected.

articles.title: Differential effects of individual versus consensus evaluations of narrator-to-story fit on the experience and outcomes of narrative listening.
articles.authors: Carolyn McGettigan; Khadija Faiz; Amy Francis; Elizabeth Leivers; Laurie Sin; Hannah Jones; Nadine Lavan; Saloni Krishnan
articles.abstract: While a reader might imagine the narrator's and characters' voices in a written book, a spoken narrative solidifies the relationship between the narrator and the text. Here, we report two experiments investigating how perceived narrator-to-story fit affects narrative listening enjoyment and other listening outcomes. In a first experiment (N=400 participants), we manipulated the gender-related congruence between the expected and heard narrator of four spoken narratives in a willingness-to-wait paradigm. We found that listeners were more likely to continue listening to congruent than incongruent stories, but did not enjoy them more or comprehend them more accurately. However, we observed a dissociation in the observed effects of perceived narrator-to-story fit: specifically, higher individual evaluations significantly increased enjoyment, while both higher individual and (aggregated) mean fit ratings predicted greater motivation to continue listening. This suggested that crowd-sourced data may be less effective than personal taste when predicting narrative listening enjoyment. Indeed, a second experiment using a larger number of stories showed that participants’ enjoyment of spoken narratives is most strongly predicted by within-sample individual fit ratings, but not by within- or between-group aggregate ratings. Our findings provide evidence to support personalisation of narration as a way to promote enjoyment of spoken narratives and, potentially, audiobooks.

articles.title: Thematic structure and pause duration shape event segmentation during speech listening in younger and older adults
articles.authors: Yulia Lamekina; Ryan Panela; Carolyn Kortje; Ingrid Johnsrude; Bjorn Herrmann
articles.abstract: Event segmentation – the division of continuous experience into meaningful units – is essential for understanding narratives. Yet little is known about how listeners segment auditory stories, how prosodic cues such as pauses contribute, and how age-related changes in hearing and cognition affect this process. We conducted two experiments to address these questions. In Experiment 1, human and advanced AI voices for audiobooks and podcast monologues produced longer pauses at thematic event boundaries than within events, indicating that pause timing aligns with narrative structure. In Experiment 2, younger (19–35 years old) and older (56–79 years old) adults listened to stories in which pauses were selectively prolonged at event boundaries or event centers. Older adults identified event boundaries more frequently overall. Prolonging pauses at event boundaries did not enhance boundary identification, whereas prolonging pauses at event centers led to boundary identification despite the absence of a major thematic shift, particularly in listeners with poorer hearing. Hence, aging may change the sensitivity to event boundaries during continuous speech listening, and pause duration can bias event segmentation when thematic cues are absent.

articles.title: Common psychiatric treatments alter affective dynamics
articles.authors: Quentin Dercon; Quentin JM Huys; Robb Rutledge; Camilla Nord
articles.abstract: Affective states are dynamic, fluctuating in response to recent events: an unexpected pleasure, a disappointing loss. Affective biases, which cause disruptions in these dynamics, are core components of mental ill-health, but the specific effects of treatments on these biases are poorly understood. Here, we investigate the impact of common psychiatric treatments on subjective assessments of happiness, confidence, and engagement during a reinforcement learning task (N=935; 130 taking antidepressant medications). Half (N=459) of the participants were randomised to practice a common psychotherapeutic technique—cognitive distancing—throughout the task. From a joint computational model of learning and affect, we find evidence for distinct and overlapping impacts of psychiatric treatments on affective dynamics. Cognitive distancing attenuates downward drift in happiness and engagement and increases recency bias in the affective impact of recent choices. Conversely, antidepressant use increases baseline happiness and confidence in individuals with similar levels of current symptoms, and decreases recency bias such that more past events influence affective states. Crucially, both cognitive distancing and antidepressant use converge to dampen negative biases in happiness and confidence specifically in participants experiencing higher levels of anxiety and depression symptoms. Together, our results indicate that common treatments for mental ill-health may alter symptoms through their impact on affective dynamics, but via distinct mechanisms.

articles.title: A Relevance Rate Model of the affective mechanisms linking social media use to later attentional disruption
articles.authors: Hippolyte Fournier; eva pool; David Sander; Elise Dan Glauser
articles.abstract: Social media use is increasingly suspected of harming attention, but the evidence remains too limited to draw any firm conclusions. One obstacle is the lack of a framework specifying how such use might affect attention afterwards, without any device. To address this gap, we draw on emotional attention, the affective mechanism that prioritises what matters to individuals. The Relevance Rate Model rests on the relevance rate, the frequency with which an environment delivers concern-relevant stimuli. Drawing on predictive coding, we suggest that social media raises the rate that users expect, and that this expectation may persist after each session and, with repeated use, across daily life. When an activity delivers less concern-relevant information than expected, sustained attention to the ongoing task may be disrupted as emotional attention is recruited to address the shortfall. The model specifies four measurable parameters of use, from which we derive a research agenda.

articles.title: Longitudinal Dataset of Psychological Variables Influencing AI Perception and Usage
articles.authors: Angelica Lermann Henestrosa; Gerrit Anders; Nico Ehrhardt; Anna Christina Faller; Nora Hampel; Irena Vanessa Ivan; Stefanie Helene Klein; Teresa Luther; Mike Prentice; Busra Sarigul
articles.abstract: Since the emergence of large language models (LLMs) in 2022, generative artificial intelligence (AI) has rapidly expanded into mainstream applications, leading, for example, to the integration of Apple Intelligence into customer devices in 2024. This integration into personal technology marks a significant shift and a further reduction in barriers to use, bringing advanced AI capabilities into everyday devices and making them accessible to private individuals. Thus, the use of generative AI along with interaction through LLM-powered (voice) assistants and engagement with AI-generated content is expected to increase significantly. However, data that link this usage to psychological variables and shed light on the underlying mechanisms of this use over time remain scarce. In this longitudinal study, data from a US-American sample was collected across six waves at two-month intervals between September 2024 and July 2025. It examines user behavior, attitudes, knowledge, and perceptions related to generative AI. Thus, this dataset allows for future research on psychological and behavioral dynamics of AI usage over time, offering insights into user engagement and the individual factors connected to it.

articles.title: Noticing yourself perceiving: Embodied reflexivity, experience design, and evidence at a free arts–science exhibition in India
articles.authors: Kohinoor Monish Darda; Hansika Mangwani; Sanjana Edwankar; Sakina Bharmal; Tanvi Raghuram; Siyona Varghese; Samrddhee Pathare; Amisha Keshan; Ritika Deshpande; Sakshi Kharbanda
articles.abstract: This study evaluates Art of Perception, a seven-zone attraction presented at Creative Lab Festival 2026 in Pune, India. A convergent mixed-methods design combined matched pre-post surveys from 200 visitors (166 complete cases) with learning statements, 1,339 face-judgment votes, and 65 post-workshop drawings. Five of six self-report outcomes showed positive paired differences after Holm correction. Bodily relaxation showed the largest difference (22.9 points on a 0-100 scale; standardised difference = 0.69); trust in perception did not differ reliably. Data indicated learning about perception, neuroplasticity, art-brain relations, and nature connection. The observational, immediate, and self-reported design does not establish causation or durability. The paper proposes a public laboratory of perception as a provisional framework for construct-aligned attraction design and evaluation.

articles.title: From Echo Chambers to Echo Machines? Endorsement, Evidence, and the Certainty of Belief in Conversations With AI
articles.authors: Olivier LE BON; Xavier Noël
articles.abstract: Randomized trials show that conversations with large language models (LLMs) can reduce conspiracy belief and, more modestly, political polarization. Yet the same systems can increase conspiracy belief when instructed to, and clinical reports describe chatbot conversations accompanying the escalation of implausible convictions. Prevailing accounts attribute both outcomes to the evidence a model supplies. We note that most experiments confound evidence about the world with endorsement of the person, and that the clearest attempt to separate them favors evidence. Drawing on research on attitude certainty, self-validation, and responses to flattery, we distinguish the position of a belief from the certainty with which it is held and formalize γ, an effect of endorsement on certainty at fixed factual content, interpretable as a validation gain. If higher certainty lowers responsiveness to later evidence, the account permits a conditional outcome: beliefs that become less extreme yet more rigid, without any misinformation. We specify two critical experiments, a factorial test of facts and endorsement that includes a source known to approve everyone and an endorsement-first design with counterevidence held constant, plus an articulation control. Conversational AI becomes a test bench for an old question: can social approval make subsequent evidence matter less?

articles.title: People Expect Less but Show Equal Influence of LLM Versus Human Moral Advice
articles.authors: Neele Engelmann; Eva-Madeleine Schmidt; Ali Alhosseini; Ivar Rodríguez Hannikainen; Mengchen Dong
articles.abstract: People are often skeptical of AI in the moral domain, yet AI-generated ethical advice can influence moral judgments as much as human advice. Unlike most prior work, which attaches human or AI labels to identical advice, we examined how much real advice written by humans and by AI influences moral judgments, and whether people expect less influence from AI than from human advice. First, we developed 24 realistic everyday moral scenarios and collected over 500 persuasive advice texts from both incentivized human writers (N = 92) and GPT-4o. AI-generated advice was longer, more linguistically complex, more semantically uniform, more virtue-oriented, and less extreme than human advice. Next, a new sample of participants (N = 390) either revised initial moral judgments after receiving human or AI advice or indicated how much they expected such advice to influence them. Participants were equally influenced by human and AI moral advice, revising their judgments by a little under a third of the distance to the advice. Participants who only estimated the influence, however, expected less influence from AI than from human advice. These findings suggest that skepticism toward AI in moral contexts may shape people's expectations about AI moral advice, but not how much they are actually influenced by it.

articles.title: Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients and spectral features directly drive micro-level autonomic reflexes during brief respiration practices
articles.authors: Jung-tzu Chang; Zai-Fu Yao
articles.abstract:
While digital health platforms increasingly deliver guided mindful breathing interventions via audio, the specific acoustic properties of the guidance are fundamentally ignored as potential active ingredients. This within-subject study implemented an unprecedented high-density experimental design to investigate how distinct, computationally engineered acoustic features (e.g., pitch, zero-crossing rate, natural background sounds) modulate acute cardiovascular, respiratory, and autonomic responses. To rigorously eliminate sex-related physiological variance, 21 meditation-naïve female university students completed 13 randomized audio sessions of a standardized 4-minute-and-5-second guided breathing practice (yielding 273 high-density recording epochs). Multiparametric biosignals, including pulse rate variability (PRV), respiratory dynamics, and electrodermal activity (EDA), were continuously recorded. Results demonstrated a robust reduction in blood pressure independent of audio conditions, confirming the fundamental efficacy of a single bout of spontaneous breath awareness. However, high-resolution analyses revealed a highly modular architecture where peripheral
autonomic indices (EDA and PRV) were acutely sensitive to fine-grained acoustic features, specifically Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs). Furthermore, physiological coupling patterns reorganized dynamically depending strictly on the acoustic context. These indings fundamentally challenge the assumption that meditation audio is a neutral delivery medium, establishing acoustic parameters as potent, independent modulators of human autonomic reflexes for future digital therapeutics.

articles.title: When the brain can change: effects of neuroplasticity education on beliefs about brain-based mental disorders
articles.authors: Olha Guley; Elena Pasquinelli; Daniel Nettle
articles.abstract: Mental disorders are increasingly framed as brain-based, which can promote pessimism about recovery. We tested whether brief education about neuroplasticity, the brain’s capacity to change throughout life, can counter these beliefs. Across three preregistered vignette experiments with UK adults (Ns = 414, 411, and 418), participants viewed a brain-framed mental disorder after either a brief neuroplasticity video and text intervention or a matched control. The intervention increased the perceived possibility of recovery, but this effect was short-lived after a single exposure in Study 1 and more durable with a booster in Study 2. The effect in Study 3 was not significant, but a pooled analysis of data from Studies 2 and 3 confirmed the positive effect overall. The intervention did not affect perceived treatment efficacy, nor did it reduce desired social distance from people with mental disorders. In Study 3, higher familiarity with the disorder was associated with a higher perceived recovery and lower desired social distance. These findings suggest neuroplasticity education can increase public optimism about recovery from mental disorders, but changing treatment beliefs or social attitudes may require more targeted interventions.

articles.title: The use of Grammatical Gender in Predictive language comprehension: Evidence from Young and Older adults
articles.authors: Anurag; Niharika Singh
articles.abstract:
Prediction-by-association, in which a word pre-activates lexically associated words, is thought to be relatively automatic and therefore spared in healthy aging. In languages with grammatical gender, however, prenominal modifiers carry both semantic and gender information, so it remains unclear whether older adults also use morphosyntactic agreement to anticipate upcoming words. We tested whether younger (n = 32, 20–35 years) and older (n = 31, 55–75 years) native Hindi speakers use the meaning and the gender marking of a prenominal adjective to anticipate an upcoming noun. In a visual-world eye-tracking task, participants heard sentences such as Abhi aap ek nukili wali sui dekhenge ('Now you will see a pointed needle') while viewing a target (needle), an adjective competitor that was semantically compatible with the adjective but mismatched its gender (spear), and two unrelated distractors. In both age groups, the target and the adjective competitor attracted comparable anticipatory fixations shortly after the adjective onset, and both were fixated more than the distractors. Later in the pre-noun interval, fixations to the target began to exceed those to the gender-mismatching competitor, although this advantage was modest. None of these effects interacted with age group, and filler sentences without a predictive adjective elicited no anticipatory fixations. These findings suggest that early anticipation is driven primarily by lexical-semantic association, with grammatical gender constraining predictions somewhat later, and that neither source of information shows age-related decline in contextually simple sentences.
Keywords: prediction; aging; grammatical gender; visual world paradigm; eye-tracking; Hindi

articles.title: Mapping Social Determinants of Health in Pediatric Populations: A Scoping Review
articles.authors: Amy Jolin; Sarah Caimano; Karen Arias; Ashley Toombs-Heavisides; Christina Ghaleb; Laurence Kirmayer; Jacob A. Burack; Tasmia Hai
articles.abstract: Social determinants of health (SDH) are increasingly recognized as essential for understanding health outcomes across public health and social sciences. In pediatric health, the importance of addressing SDH is particularly evident, as early-life exposure to adverse social conditions can have lifelong impacts on health. However, there is significant variation in how researchers conceptualize and measure SDH, which presents considerable challenges in translating evidence into practice. Using the PROGRESS-Plus framework, we conducted a scoping review to explore how research conceptualized and measured SDH in pediatric studies. We identified 10,268 empirical, peer-reviewed studies that were published in English, focused on populations under 18 years of age, and examined social determinants of health. A total of 316 articles were included in this review, highlighting the widespread use of the term in the literature. Results indicated substantial variability in the SDH factors and measurement approaches used across studies, with few studies examining two or more factors (21%). Additionally, many researchers were not explicit about what they considered SDH. They often used the term without a definition and explanation of what the term meant in the context of their research. Socioeconomic status (26.8%), education (17.9%) and social capital (13.1) were among the most frequently used factors when assessing SDH. Based on this review, we present recommendations for strengthening the conceptualization and measurement of SDH in future research involving pediatric populations.

articles.title: People Offload Empathy to AI
articles.authors: Madhulika Shastry; Kurt Gray
articles.abstract: Giving empathy is good, but providing emotional support is hard work. Empathic AI gives cheap and easy support, but may be ethically costly. When AI provides empathy, people may feel less compelled to support others. Four studies provide evidence for “empathy offloading:” when people see AI as capable of empathy, they become less willing to empathize with the suffering of others, even without realizing it. When AI seems more capable of empathy people—both with correlations (Study 1) and causal experiments (Study 2)—people report more empathy offloading. When people learn that someone has received emotional support from large language models (LLMs), they engage less with others’ mental states (Study 3) and offer fewer empathic responses (Study 4). Empathic AI might provide low-cost, easily accessible emotional support, but it risks fraying the ethical and emotional commitments we make to other humans. When someone can go cry to AI, why bother getting splashed with their tears?

articles.title: Predictors of Reading and Spelling ability in adults: Phonological skills outweigh Visual Attention Span
articles.authors: Jennifer Burt; Jo-Maree Ceccato; Jack Mitchell Ingram Leggett
articles.abstract: According to the Visual attention span (VAS) hypothesis, the ability to identify a briefly presented sequence of visual elements (usually consonants) aids reading acquisition independently of skills related to the sounds of a language (phonology). A new test with a reduced memory load addressed concerns about a phonological memory confound in traditional VAS tests. In this PreProbe test, a probe letter was presented before each trial and the task was to decide whether it occurred in the brief five-letter sequence. A correlational study with 264 adults assessed the relationships of VAS, phonological skills, and print exposure with both word-reading and spelling. Both PreProbe and the traditional partial report VAS (PosProbe) had modest correlations with the literacy measures, and also with the measures of phonological skills. In regression analyses, two phonological measures explained over 30% of literacy variance independently of VAS, while each VAS measure uniquely explained a maximum of 3%. VAS may reflect achievement in phonological and literacy skills, and has at best a minor causal role in literacy.

articles.title: To replicate or not to replicate? My nine failures to publish a successful replication
articles.authors: Sharon Gilaie-Dotan
articles.abstract: Simmons, Nelson, and Simonsohn (2011) proposed disclosure-based practices — a priori power analyses, full reporting of conditions and exclusions, results reported with and without exclusions applied — as a remedy for the replication crisis. Following these practices explicitly, our lab attempted to publish an online replication and extension of our earlier PNAS findings on image size and memory, expecting that doing so would make publication straightforward. It did not. Nine submissions over 2.5 years were unsuccessful (eight rejections and one withdrawal), largely on the grounds that a transparent, successful replication lacked sufficient theoretical novelty to warrant publication on its own; it was accepted only after this framing was substantially minimized in favor of additional analyses and an alternative theoretical framework. Here, I reflect on this experience, raise open questions about whether the field's evaluation of replications has kept pace with its stated commitment to them, and offer recommendations for future practices.

articles.title: When an integration composite fails to cohere: host-language orientation as social-world affiliation, and the formative logic behind a failed scale
articles.authors: Shiyun Zhang Isabelle
articles.abstract: Surveys often treat international students' host-language use and "integration" items as measures of one disposition. This article asks what such items measure, and what it means when they fail to cohere. It draws on an explanatory sequential mixed-methods study at a national research university in Japan during the shift to online teaching. The data are a survey of international students (N = 176) and 39 interviews with 40 students. Choice of the Japanese survey form was the outcome. Region of origin dominated that choice (Sinosphere odds ratio ≈ 16.2). Three integration indicators were small, could not be separated from origin, and did not cohere (alpha = 0.36). The interviews suggest that the indicators are formative traces of a clustered social world, not reflections of one trait. For such indicators, internal consistency is the wrong test. A low alpha should prompt the question of what the items jointly index.

articles.title: The Role of Parental Reflective Functioning in the Association Between Parental and Youth Emotion Regulation Among Youth With Serious Mental Health Challenges
articles.authors: Laura Daari; Sebastian Dys; Marlene Moretti
articles.abstract:
Background: Parental and adolescent emotion regulation are associated, yet the role of parental reflective functioning (PRF) as a relational pathway linking them remains largely unexamined, particularly among parents of youth with serious mental health challenges.

Methods: Parents (N = 372) of adolescents (ages 9–19) with serious mental health challenges reported on their own emotion regulation within the parent–adolescent relationship, PRF, and their adolescent's emotion regulation. Structural equation modelling with bootstrapped indirect effects examined direct and indirect associations between parental emotion regulation (dysregulation, suppression), PRF facets (prementalizing, certainty about mental states, and interest and curiosity in mental states), and adolescent emotion regulation (dysregulation, suppression). 

Results: Parental dysregulation was positively associated with adolescent dysregulation and suppression, whereas parental suppression showed no direct associations with adolescent outcomes. All three PRF facets were associated with adolescent emotion regulation: greater prementalizing with greater youth dysregulation; greater certainty with lower youth dysregulation and suppression; and greater interest and curiosity unexpectedly with greater youth dysregulation and suppression. Three indirect associations emerged: parental dysregulation was associated with adolescent dysregulation through higher prementalizing and, separately, through lower certainty about mental states, and parental suppression was associated with lower adolescent suppression through lower interest and curiosity.

Conclusions:  Parental dysregulation was associated with adolescent emotion regulation in this clinical sample, relating to adolescent dysregulation through both prementalizing and certainty. Less consistent with prior research, interest and curiosity was associated with poorer adolescent emotion regulation, raising the possibility that this facet relates differently in clinical, adolescent populations than in the community samples of younger children where it has typically been studied. These findings suggest PRF facets may represent differentiated intervention targets, and highlight the need for longitudinal, multi-informant research to establish temporal ordering.

Keywords: emotion regulation; parental reflective functioning; mentalizing; parenting; adolescents; parent–child relationship

articles.title: Language-Based Mental Health Assessments Do Not Perform Evenly Across Racial and Ethnic Groups
articles.authors: Steven Mesquiti; Rebecca Carey; Nathaniel Daw; Erik C Nook
articles.abstract: Psycholinguistic tools that estimate psychological symptoms from language alone aim to provide unobtrusive assessments without needing questionnaires or clinicians. Researchers largely assume that these assessments function equivalently across demographic groups. We tested this assumption in a racially diverse sample of U.S. adults (N = 1,685; Black, Asian, Latino/Hispanic, White) who described their mental health and completed standard symptom questionnaires. Language-based markers of internalizing symptoms were often group-specific: First-person pronoun use predicted symptoms only among White participants, and sentiment varied in how strongly it tracked symptoms across groups. Machine learning models trained on White participants' language produced higher prediction error for other groups than those groups' own models did. Interpretability techniques revealed that White-trained models emphasized self-focused, agentic language more than minority groups' models. These findings indicate that linguistic tools cannot assume generalizability and must be evaluated for the populations they serve.

articles.title: Cross-Modal Associations in Creativity: Evaluating Word-Image Pairing in Humans and Large Language Models
articles.authors: Eva Illion; Linxuan Wang; Liane Gabora
articles.abstract: Given differences in the associative memory architectures of humans and AI, it is not clear whether AI generates and interprets visual-linguistic associations the way humans do. To investigate this, human participants and two large language models (LLMs), ChatGPT and Gemini, were asked to generate novel words and corresponding images that form meaningfully linked dyads. The LLMs and a second group of human participants were presented with shuffled sets of these words and images and asked to rematch them in ways they felt were most meaningful. Humans performed similarly regardless of whether the pairs were human or LLM-generated, while LLMs were better at matching LLM-generated pairs. Overall, LLMs outperformed humans at recovering the intended pairings. These findings suggest that despite architectural differences, the way in which AI generates and detects associations between language and visual stimuli is not only like that of humans, but they may be superior at recognizing cross-domain associations that humans find meaningful.

articles.title: Should AI Trust Its Gut?  The Cost of Deliberative Moral Reasoning in Humans and AI
articles.authors: Simon Myers; Nick Chater
articles.abstract: People prefer deliberation to intuition, when judging how others solve hard problems, and they extend this to artificial agents. Yet in the moral domain, the preference may reverse as intuitive moral responses appear to signal good character. One explanation is that fast, intuitive responses show real emotional engagement. Since machines are thought to lack emotion, it is unclear whether a preference for intuition in the moral domain extends to AI. Across three preregistered studies (N = 2,173), we find that it does, but that it appears to be driven by commitment to moral norms and precedents rather than emotion. In Study 1, participants preferred intuitive reasoning for moral decisions and systematic reasoning for non-moral decisions, for human and AI agents alike. Intuitive moral reasoning signalled better character but was not clearly expected to produce better outcomes. In Study 2, the character preference persisted when the AI was described as being incapable of emotion. In Study 3, we held the decision fixed and varied how firmly the agent held the relevant moral norm. An agent who would never reconsider applying a moral norm was rated above one who would reconsider given sufficiently high stakes; and both above one who weighed costs and benefits case by case. Commitment raised character ratings more than expected-outcome ratings. The character-based cost of moral deliberation appears to be a cost of treating a moral norm as negotiable, and we found strong evidence that people apply this inference to machines and people alike.

articles.title: Benchmarking and Quantifying Facial Motion With Controlled Photorealistic Avatars
articles.authors: Hilal Nizamoğlu; Peer Herholz; Katharina Dobs
articles.abstract: Facial expressions are central to human social interaction, yet reliably quantifying how faces move over time remains challenging. Here, we address these limitations in three ways. First, we leverage photorealistic MetaHuman animations with precisely specified facial motion to systematically evaluate two widely used AU detection systems: AFAR and OpenFace. Four avatars were animated with identical motion parameters to generate 72 videos comprising single-AU and AU-combination sequences. Although both systems performed above chance, their performance varied substantially across AUs and avatars. Second, we introduce and validate a complementary landmark-displacement approach that directly quantifies nonrigid facial motion from tracked geometry, yielding consistent and robust motion estimates across avatars and animations. Third, we provide FACET, an open-source toolbox that integrates AU detection and landmark-based motion analysis within a unified and reproducible framework. Together, our findings reveal systematic biases in current AU-detection systems, highlight the potential of landmark-based analysis to characterize facial motion directly, and provide an open, reproducible framework for quantifying facial motion and evaluating the methods used to capture it.

articles.title: Translational neuroscience in psychoeducation: Mapping nonmotor circuitry to clinical management in movement disorders
articles.authors: Behzad Elahi
articles.abstract:
Non-motor symptoms (NMS) affect nearly all patients with Parkinson’s disease (PD)
and related movement disorders, with a mean of roughly 8–10 discrete symptoms per
individual. Their effect on quality of life often exceeds that of motor features, yet
NMS remain under-recognized and undertreated, partly because patients and caregivers lack a working model of why these symptoms arise in a “movement” disease.
This chapter applies neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) to that gap and
positions it relative to conventional psychoeducation, health communication, and behavioral science. We propose the Map-Normalize-Differentiate-Navigate (MNDN)
workflow as a movement-disorders-specific implementation of the NIPE framework
described in Chapter 1 of this volume. MNDN is a clinical proposal, not a validated
protocol: its components are specified so that it can be tested, but its effects on patient outcomes have not been evaluated. Drawing on the tripartite cortico-basal ganglia-thalamocortical loop model and multi-transmitter degeneration, we provide modules for seven high-yield NMS: apathy, anxiety, executive dysfunction, REM sleep
behavior disorder, neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, psychosis, and fatigue. Each
module summarizes the neural systems implicated, at the level of certainty the evidence supports, together with common misattributions, reversible contributors that
must be excluded, management options and their limits, and patient and caregiver
handout content. We describe delivery formats from 3 to 5 min “micro-NIPE” sessions in routine visits to group and telehealth programs, specify the minimum components, provider competencies, dose, fidelity criteria, and proximal outcomes needed
to test MNDN, and examine the ethical risks of neurobiological framing (determinism, oversimplification, over-attribution, and false reassurance), with particular attention to prognostic counseling in REM sleep behavior disorder. NIPE in movement
disorders is designed to reduce self-blame, support accurate symptom attribution, and
improve collaborative management. Whether it does so is an empirical question that
this chapter aims to make answerable.

articles.title: Disentangling Political Polarization in the Context of Personalized Information Environments: The Effects of Attitudinal Congruence and the Role of Individual Differences
articles.authors: Solange Vega Yanez; Cornelia Sindermann
articles.abstract: Personalized information environments have been proposed to contribute to political polarization, yet empirical findings remain mixed. The present work aimed to clarify these inconsistencies by distinguishing between different polarization outcomes and considering individual characteristics as potential moderators. In an online experiment, we tested how attitude-congruency of information environments affects issue and affective polarization regarding unconditional basic income (UBI) in Germany, and whether Intellectual Humility (IH) and Need for Cognitive Closure (NfCC) moderate these effects. N = 756 participants were exposed to one of three information environments containing predominantly attitude-congruent, attitude-incongruent, or neutral statements about UBI. Affective polarization was assessed separately as the divide in negative affective evaluations (stronger negative feelings toward the outgroup than ingroup; NAD) and the divide in positive affective evaluations (PAD; stronger positive feelings toward the ingroup than outgroup) between issue-based groups. Compared with neutral exposure, attitude-congruent information increased issue polarization, NAD, and PAD. Attitude-incongruent information decreased issue polarization but  had no signficant effect on either affective divide. IH was positively associated with and moderated effects on PAD. NfCC showed no effects. Findings highlight the importance of distinguishing between polarization outcomes and suggest that positive and negative affective intergroup divides may show different associations with individual characteristics.

articles.title: Impaired Updating and Maintenance of Latent Structural Associations Underlie Cognitive Inflexibility along an Obsessive–Compulsive Dimension
articles.authors: Georgios Tertikas; Nadescha Trudel; Tricia Xing Fang Seow; Miriam Klein-Flugge; Tobias U. Hauser
articles.abstract: Impaired cognitive flexibility, the ability to form and update latent structural associations, is a hallmark of psychiatric conditions such as obsessive-compulsive (OC) disorder, yet its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Using a novel structural inference task, we dissociated three candidate mechanisms: (i) initial acquisition of associative structures, (ii) belief updating following structural changes, and (iii) inference about unobserved associations. In a large general-population sample (N=313), transdiagnostically characterised OC symptoms were linked to impaired updating following structural change and reduced generalisation to unobserved associations, whilst initial learning remained intact. Using fMRI (N=51), we found this was driven by overrepresenting structurally irrelevant associations in medial orbitofrontal cortex, and impaired formation of novel latent associations in posterior hippocampus. These findings reveal that OC-related cognitive inflexibility is grounded in dissociable fronto-hippocampal representational failures that impair structural model revision, rather than the capacity to acquire latent associations in the first place.

articles.title: Expanding the Multimodal Framework of Workplace Ostracism: Integrating Linguistic Ostracism as a Distinct Modality
articles.authors: No authors listed
articles.abstract: While research on workplace ostracism has largely focused on social, physical, and cyber modalities, emerging scholarship highlights linguistic ostracism as a distinct and under-recognized modality. It presents unique complexities due to its high attributional ambiguity, generally non-purposeful nature, and the requirement that a subgroup of two or more individuals speak a shared language unfamiliar to the target. This chapter proposes a multimodal perspective on workplace ostracism by situating linguistic ostracism alongside social, physical, and cyber modalities. Through a comparative analysis of these four modalities, the chapter identifies both shared aspects and key points of divergence. It also considers how they may interact, potentially amplifying their impact when they co-occur. By positioning linguistic ostracism as a complementary and essential form, the chapter aims to expand current theoretical frameworks and underscore the value of a multimodal approach to understanding workplace ostracism, particularly in linguistically and culturally diverse work environments.

articles_hidden.title: Examining the Role of Working Memory in Reasoning and Meta-reasoning:  A Fuzzy-trace approach
articles_hidden.authors: Leili Rouhi; Zuleykha Gasimova; Valerie A Thompson
articles_hidden.abstract: Meta-reasoning, the ability to monitor progress and regulate effort during reasoning, comprises monitoring and control. Monitoring, including confidence, is assumed to guide control processes. Yet, whether monitoring and control compete with reasoning for shared cognitive resources is unclear. To address this, we examined the role of working memory in reasoning and meta-reasoning, drawing on Fuzzy Trace Theory and the meta-reasoning framework. Participants (N = 998) solved syllogisms with and without validity-believability conflict in a two-response paradigm under six constraint conditions. Accuracy declined only when load and deadline were combined. Confidence was lower on conflict than on non-conflict problems and reliably predicted answer changes and rethinking time across all conditions. Monitoring resolution, however, was low throughout. These results suggest cognitive constraints impair reasoning generally but largely spare conflict-detection and control sensitivity. Reasoners’ limited ability to discriminate correct from incorrect responses appears to reflect a general monitoring limitations rather than constrained resources.

articles_hidden.title: Avoiding Feelings and Resisting Closeness: A Network Analysis of Attachment and Affect Regulation in Adolescents with Mental Health Concerns
articles_hidden.authors: Sherene Balanji; Marlene Moretti
articles_hidden.abstract: Adolescents with mental health concerns often experience difficulties navigating attachment relationships and regulating emotions. Although attachment insecurity and affect regulation difficulties are well-established transdiagnostic risk factors for adolescent psychopathology, far less is known about the specific experiences and beliefs that connect these domains. Understanding these connections may provide insight into how attachment insecurity and affect regulation difficulties mutually reinforce one another. The present study used a cross-sectional network analysis to examine item-level associations among attachment and affect regulation in a clinical sample of 608 adolescents (57% female; Mage = 13.98, SD = 2.36) referred to publicly funded youth mental health services. Community detection analyses identified four interconnected dimensions corresponding to attachment anxiety, attachment avoidance, affect dysregulation/suppression, and affect reflection. Notably, affect dysregulation and suppression formed a unified community when examined alongside attachment, suggesting that emotional overwhelm and emotional avoidance may function as closely interconnected aspects of emotional functioning. Two bridge nodes emerged as key points of connection between attachment and affect regulation: the belief that “thinking about my feelings just makes everything worse” and the experience of wanting closeness with a parent while simultaneously pulling away. These findings highlight beliefs about emotions and uncertainty regarding interpersonal closeness and support as important points of connection between attachment insecurity and affect regulation difficulties. Implications for attachment-informed intervention and future research are discussed.

articles_hidden.title: Underestimating the replicability of the social and behavioural sciences: an audit of six surprising SCORE replication failures.
articles_hidden.authors: Shaheed Azaad
articles_hidden.abstract: The Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence (SCORE) project recently published a large-scale replication project within the social and behavioural sciences. The authors replicated only 151 of 274 (55%) claims, a finding covered by major outlets such as the New York Times and Forbes. Here, I audited SCORE replications of six studies where at least one claim surprisingly failed to replicate. These failures were surprising because the original study produced a p < .01 while the replication yielded a significant effect in the opposite direction. I show that, of the 12 claims tested across these six replications, five were miscategorised as failed replications because of data analysis and interpretation problems, and six replications were invalid because of poor data quality and an error in the replication’s experiment code. I conclude that individual replications within replicability projects may benefit from more thorough peer review, and that a more comprehensive audit is necessary before we can be confident in the project’s overall replicability estimate.

articles_hidden.title: The social ecology of development: The changing structure of preschoolers’ everyday experiences at home
articles_hidden.authors: Nele-Pauline Suffo; Anas Suffo; Pierre-Etienne Martin; Yujin Kim; Anam Zahra; Daniel Haun; Manuel Bohn
articles_hidden.abstract: Everyday social interactions shape human psychological development. Research, however, has primarily relied on controlled settings or brief observations; consequently, the nature of naturalistic everyday experiences remains largely unstudied. To address this gap, we developed an automated multimodal processing pipeline to analyze a large egocentric corpus of naturalistic everyday experiences from 107 children aged three to five years in Germany (267.52 hours). The pipeline detects faces, persons, proximity, and speech types to classify time into interacting, available, or alone states. Results indicate a significant ecological reorganization: social interaction dominates at age three and declines towards a more even distribution between states at age six. Conversational agency remains stable throughout preschool, with children sharing it nearly equally with conversational partners. Crucially, social interactions change in their structure in that isolated social cues become significantly less predictive of interactions with age. Thus, preschool social interactions become less frequent but more diverse with development.

articles_hidden.title: Examining Physiological Hyperarousal in the Relationship Between Insomnia and Nightmare Proneness
articles_hidden.authors: William E. Kelly; Ani Enriquez; Faith Yanez
articles_hidden.abstract: Nightmare proneness has been associated with insomnia beyond nightmare frequency and neuroticism. The present study examined physiological hyperarousal as a potential process contributing to this relationship. Participants were 209 adults recruited from a university participant pool and an online community sample. Participants completed self-report measures of nightmare proneness, insomnia, physiological hyperarousal, nightmare frequency, neuroticism, and trauma symptoms. Hierarchical regression and indirect-effect analyses were conducted. After controlling for recruitment source, age, gender, nightmare frequency, neuroticism, and trauma symptoms, nightmare proneness explained an additional 6.5% of the variance in insomnia. Physiological hyperarousal accounted for an additional 2.3% of variance beyond nightmare proneness. Nightmare proneness showed a significant indirect association with insomnia through physiological hyperarousal but maintained a direct association with insomnia after physiological hyperarousal was considered. Physiological hyperarousal may represent one process contributing to the relationship between nightmare proneness and insomnia but does not fully account for this association. The findings support conceptualizing nightmare proneness and physiological hyperarousal as related but non-redundant factors associated with insomnia.

articles_hidden.title: Age-Related Neural Dedifferentiation Is Driven by Declining Reliability
articles_hidden.authors: Tiantian Yang; Molly Simmonite; Ethan Maddox; Bingjie Liu; Thad Polk
articles_hidden.abstract:
Neural dedifferentiation, characterized by reduced distinctiveness of neural representations, is a robust feature of cognitive aging. Multivoxel pattern analyses often operationalize neural distinctiveness as the difference between within-category similarity (reliability) and between-category similarity (confusability). However, it remains unclear whether age-related reductions in distinctiveness are driven by decreases in reliability, increases in confusability, or both, and whether these components demonstrate similar longitudinal trajectories. Using cross-sectional and longitudinal data from the Michigan Neural Distinctiveness (MiND) study, we decomposed distinctiveness into its two components across visual, auditory, and motor cortex in more than 200 young (18-29 years) and older adults (65-94 years) and estimated cross-sectional between-person age differences and longitudinal within-person change simultaneously in mixed-effects models. We found that reliability was lower in older vs. younger adults cross-sectionally, and this reduction was significantly larger than the corresponding effect on confusability. Moreover, reliability also declined longitudinally within individuals across a mean interval of four years. These findings indicate that age-related dedifferentiation is driven primarily by declining reliability rather than increasing confusability, and that reporting distinctiveness alone can conceal substantial age-related change in its components. 
Keywords: Dedifferentiation, distinctiveness, reliability, confusability, aging, longitudinal study

articles_hidden.title: Eye-gaze dynamics reveal the adaptive nature of real-time noisy-channel inference in speech comprehension
articles_hidden.authors: Rachel Anna Ryskin
articles_hidden.abstract: To understand spoken language, listeners must extract meaning from acoustic input that is variable and noisy. The noisy-channel framework posits that listeners overcome this uncertainty by rationally inferring the speaker's intent, combining prior expectations with a model of how the message may have been corrupted during transmission. However, the exact nature of this noise model and its sensitivity to context (e.g., speaker or acoustic environment) remain unknown. Here, I use eye-tracking to measure human speech processing as it unfolds on the millisecond timescale, and I use the representational geometry of a self-supervised speech model (HuBERT) to estimate the noise model. I show that spoken word comprehension is well captured as real-time Bayesian belief updating. Further, listeners flexibly tune their expectation of noise to the specific acoustic environment. These results extend the noisy-channel framework to the moment-by-moment comprehension of speech. More broadly, these findings demonstrate that the human language system continuously adapts its internal model to the statistical structure of the communicative environment. By linking noisy-channel inference with real-time perceptual dynamics, this work highlights the remarkable flexibility of human cognition in navigating uncertainty and opens the door to investigating internal representations in human and artificial speech recognition systems through their fine-grained temporal dynamics.

articles_hidden.title: Object recognition in autism: Shape configuration and Category-specificity
articles_hidden.authors: Christian Gerlach; Esben Helby; Linnea Brønnum Hansen; Ipek Oruc; Mette Elmose
articles_hidden.abstract: Face recognition in autism is well-researched and up to 1/3 of autistic individuals are reported to have severe face recognition difficulties. In comparison, there are few reports on object recognition performance in autism, and the findings are rather inconsistent. Here we report results from a series of object recognition tasks performed by autistic (N = 41) and matched non-autistic participants. Across tasks we varied the demand placed on perceptual differentiation, the structural similarity of the objects, and the salience and value of global shape information (the object’s bounding contour) relative to local shape information (details) in the recognition process. Our main hypothesis was that when local shape information was less salient than global shape information, and when both types of information needed to be integrated to support performance, autistic participants would perform less efficiently than non-autistic participants. This hypothesis was not fulfilled as the autistic group performed just as efficiently as the non-autistic group across all tasks. We discuss our findings in the context of previous reports of object recognition performance in autism and argue that former reports of impairments might reflect lexico-semantic rather than perceptual processes.

articles_hidden.title: Cultural Models of Everyday Love in Contemporary Spain: A Mixed-Methods Cultural Consensus Study
articles_hidden.authors: Saida Heshmati; Jaymes Paolo Rombaoa; Lindy Williams; Dana Hussein; Carmen Goicoechea; Andrew Villamil; Catalina LeeAnn Oselio; Saina Salamati; Corey Abramson; Martín Sánchez-Jankowski
articles_hidden.abstract: Love can emerge through moments and interactions in our daily lives, varying across different cultural contexts. Using a sequential mixed-method approach guided by Cultural Consensus Theory (CCT; Romney et al., 1986), we examined the shared agreement on which daily life experiences evoke loving feelings in Spanish culture across two studies. In Study 1, we conducted semi-structured interviews (n = 54), two-person group interviews (n = 6), and focus groups (3–5 participants; n = 40) to explore how love manifests across different relationships in daily life in Spain. Through qualitative thematic analysis, we identified recurring experiences, centering around explicit affection, instrumental support and dependable care, quality time, and thoughtful, attentive actions. This analysis informed the development of the 61-item Felt Love Questionnaire for Spain (FLQ-Spain), which collects everyday experiences with the potential to make people feel loved within the Spanish context. In Study 2, we administered the FLQ-Spain to a representative sample of Spaniards (N = 502) to assess how likely these experiences are to elicit loving feelings in the Spanish culture. Results from cognitive psychometric analysis revealed a shared agreement in the responses. ‘Highly likely’ loving eliciting experiences were characterized by support and dependability, sharing quality time, and explicit expressions of love—and particularly so within close ties such as family, partners, and friends. Results also showed that controlling or possessive behaviors from romantic partners or familial ties were unlikely to elicit love. This investigation contributes to the understanding of the shared beliefs in love in everyday life based on the perspectives of Spanish culture.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond the Labels: Phenomenological Profiles of Lucid Dreams, Sleep Paralysis, and Sleep-Related Out-of-Body Experiences
articles_hidden.authors: Nerea L. Herrero; Samantha Lee Treasure; Cecilia Forcato
articles_hidden.abstract: Lucid dreams, sleep paralysis, and sleep-related out-of-body experiences (OBEs) are usually defined by a characteristic feature, although considerable phenomenological variability exists within each phenomenon. We explored how different experiential features were organized across participant-level profiles within these phenomena. Data came from an online survey completed by 389 adults who reported at least one of the three experiences. Separate multivariate analyses were conducted within each phenomenon using multiple correspondence analysis followed by hierarchical clustering on principal components. We examined volitional regulation, predominant affective category, and, for OBEs, embodiment-related features. In lucid dreams and OBEs, voluntary induction, agency, and environmental control did not always occur together. Consistent voluntary induction and consistent environmental control characterized different profiles in both phenomena. In OBEs, predominantly positive emotions characterized profiles with different patterns of induction and agency, whereas predominantly negative emotions characterized a profile with low volition. In sleep paralysis, predominantly negative emotions occurred across several phenomenological profiles, whereas predominantly positive emotions characterized a profile associated with vestibular-motor experiences and out-of-body feelings. Sleep-related OBEs also showed marked variability in bodily experience, including profiles characterized by consistent body ownership, variable embodiment, or no perceived body. These findings provide an exploratory description of how phenomenological features are organized across participant-level profiles within lucid dreams, sleep paralysis, and OBEs. The resulting profiles should not be considered fixed subtypes, but rather patterns to be tested in independent samples using prospective or episode-level assessments.

articles_hidden.title: Examining Linking Language and Causal Implications in Observational Psychological Capital Research
articles_hidden.authors: Elise Mockett; Matt N Williams; Dianne Gardner; Larry Paing
articles_hidden.abstract: The present study examines whether the issues with implied causal inference identified by Haber et al. (2022) in observational health research extend to the field of industrial-organisational (IO) psychology. Haber et al. found that causal relationships were implied through the language used to link exposures and outcomes and through recommendations for action. This small-scale conceptual replication applies Haber et al.’s approach to psychological capital (PsyCap), an increasingly popular construct in the domain of IO psychology. Specifically, we evaluate the causal strength of the language used to describe the nature of the connection between given variables when reporting findings and when making recommendations for action in 50 PsyCap articles. The majority of action recommendations were found to have strong causal implications (85% in abstracts, 84% in discussion sections), and most linking sentences implied some level of causality (64% in abstracts, 58% in discussion sections). This was despite very few articles explicitly stating an intention to estimate causal effects (10%) and many explicitly warning against drawing causal inferences (42%). No significant relationship was found between the causality implied in the linking sentences and the strength of causal implication of the action recommendations. These findings have important implications for how research is implemented, and very real consequences for those who are the focus of such implementations. Increased transparency about causal interests and reasoning is needed to uphold the credibility of findings and the integrity of applications of observational PsyCap research.

articles_hidden.title: Extending the Validation of the Anhedonia Scale for Adolescents into Young Adulthood: Psychometric Properties and Longitudinal Prediction of Depressive Symptoms
articles_hidden.authors: Sena Demir-Kassem; Katie Prizeman; Angad Sahni; Xueqing Ma; Manasa Veluvali; Tarun Vermani; Samantha Catherine Cacace; Ciara McCabe
articles_hidden.abstract: Anhedonia is a core symptom of depression linked to poorer outcomes in young people. The Anhedonia Scale for Adolescents (ASA) is a 14-item multidimensional measure validated in 11–18-year-olds. We examined its psychometric properties in 1,199 individuals aged 16–25 years, with and without clinical diagnoses. Confirmatory factor analysis supported the original three-factor structure over one- and two-factor alternatives. Internal consistency was excellent for the total scale (α = .92), acceptable to good for the subscales (α = .71–.88) and comparable across age and clinical groups; five-month test–retest reliability was moderate (ICC = .69). The ASA correlated with the Snaith–Hamilton Pleasure Scale (SHAPS; rₛ = .66) and depressive symptoms (rₛ = .80), explained variance in depressive symptoms beyond the SHAPS (ΔR² = .32), and predicted depressive symptoms five months later beyond baseline symptoms. The ASA is a reliable, valid measure of anhedonia across adolescence and young adulthood.

articles_hidden.title: The gender gap in math anxiety (and in the link between math anxiety and math achievement) is not so salient when other anxieties are controlled for
articles_hidden.authors: Monika Szczygieł; Mateusz Hohol
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background and Objectives: Math anxiety (MA) is considered to affect math achievement and the choice of math-related educational paths, thus contributing to the gender gap in STEM careers. However, despite decades of research, the mechanisms underlying the relationships between gender, MA, and math achievement remain largely unclear. One of the reasons is that different types of anxiety and math achievement levels are rarely controlled for.
Design and methods: We tested the associations between gender, MA, spatial anxiety, test anxiety, neuroticism, and math achievement in a sample of 269 adults. 
Results: We replicated previous findings that spatial anxiety in areas of navigation and mental manipulation, but not imagery, mediates the relationship between gender and MA. Importantly, in light of previous contradictory findings, we found that math achievement significantly mediated this relationship. Crucially, we found that gender, spatial anxiety, test anxiety, neuroticism, and math achievement together accounted for 66% of the variance in MA, with gender uniquely accounting for only 5%. 
Conclusions: The commonly reported gender gap in MA is less pronounced when other anxieties are controlled for, especially given that we did not observe gender differences in the strength of the relationship between MA and math achievement.

articles_hidden.title: Prior information about another’s emotional state shapes the perceptual representation of their facial expressions
articles_hidden.authors: Igne Jasukaityte; Margaret Cecilia Jackson; Patric Bach
articles_hidden.abstract: Context is known to change how people evaluate facial expressions. However, predictive processing  accounts  claim  that  context  should  also  shape faceperceptual  representation, causing objectively identical expressions to appear different perceptually. We tested thisin five experiments with English-speaking adults in the UK and Ireland,recruited through a university participant pool and online platforms (total N= 413; 18–49 years; data collected 2023–2026).Participants heard how a person was feeling, watched that person’s ambiguous expression change towards a congruent or incongruent emotion, and judged the expression’s final seen emotional state. Expressions were rated as happier after happystatementsand sadder after sad statements (Experiment 1a), replicating prior work. However, they were also rated as more intense when congruent with prior statements than when incongruent (Experiment 1b), ruling out biases from statement-to-response mappings. When participants perceptually compared final  expressions  with  slightly  more  or  less  expressive  probe  faces,  they  generally overestimated faceexpressiveness (Experiments 2a, 2b). Crucially, this overestimation was larger for expressionscongruent with prior expectations, but only when the probe appeared after a longer delay (1000 vs 333 ms). The same pattern emerged when the emotion was not explicitly stated but inferred from a variety of news that participants delivered to the person (Experiment 3). Prior knowledge of another’s emotional state therefore shapes notonlythe evaluation of the person’s facial expressions but also their perceptual representation, consistent with  predictive  accounts.  Generalization  to  naturalistic  expressions,  other  emotions,and cultures remains to be tested.

articles_hidden.title: Suppressing Distractors, Enhancing Targets: Template Tuning in Ensemble Perception
articles_hidden.authors: Gizem Tanseli Kaspar; Sabrina Hansmann-Roth
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Ensemble perception is a fundamental mechanism enabling the visual system to rapidly extract summary statistical properties (e.g., mean orientation) from a large number of objects. This study investigated the influence of attentional templates for targets and distractors which are formed during visual search, on subsequent ensemble perception. Participants first completed a visual search task involving target and distractor colors, followed by an ensemble orientation estimation task in which these colors recurred in various combinations. The first experiment revealed that target template systematically biased ensemble estimates, with the strongest effect occurring when both template colors recurred together. Furthermore, on these trials the bias exceeded the sum of the individual effects of target and distractor conditions, which demonstrates that combined effect of target enhancement and distractor suppression may be greater than predicted by their individual effects. In the second experiment, presentation duration (150 ms vs. 500 ms) was manipulated. While our results showed that duration did not alter the magnitude of the biases, a longer presentation time improved response precision. These findings suggest that ensemble perception can be modulated by recently formed attentional templates and systematically shape the formation of summary statistical representations.
Keywords: Ensemble Perception, Attentional Templates, Statistical Summary Representations

articles_hidden.title: Procedural learning in the serial reaction time task in individuals with and without Dyslexia: group-level and individual differences
articles_hidden.authors: Catia Margarida Oliveira; Marianna E. Hayiou-Thomas; Lisa Henderson
articles_hidden.abstract: An impairment in the procedural memory system, responsible for the extraction and assimilation of regularities from sensory input, has been suggested to play a causal role in neurodevelopmental disorders such as dyslexia. In this study, we compared the performance of adults with and without dyslexia on the Serial Reaction Time task across three sessions. Alongside it, this experiment presents the first examination of the stability of procedural learning in a dyslexic population. Across sessions, there was no evidence of an impairment in the dyslexic groups, thus lending no support to the procedural deficit hypothesis. There was limited evidence for a relationship between language/literacy abilities and procedural learning, with only a significant association between nonword repetition and procedural learning for the dyslexic group (r = .31). However, given that the reliability of the SRTT was well-below adequate psychometric standards in both groups, the lack of correlations between these measures may reflect attenuation. Nonetheless, a positive correlation between attention and procedural learning was observed in both groups, suggesting that individuals with better attentional abilities showed more evidence of procedural learning in the SRTT (rs between -.34 to -.47). In light of these findings, it is unclear whether a procedural learning impairment can account for the behavioural and cognitive profile observed in individuals with dyslexia.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond referral: Making physical activity opportunities usable in school-based social prescribing for young people experiencing loneliness
articles_hidden.authors: Robert J Booth; Nano Quirke-Bakradze; Sophie Ellis Cooper; Daisy Fancourt; Daniel Hayes
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: For young people experiencing loneliness or low community connection, physical activity may support social contact, enjoyment and belonging. Social prescribing offers a person-centred route to organised sport, exercise, active recreation and less structured movement, but identification or referral does not ensure usability. Little is known about the individual, relational, school and community conditions that make these opportunities meaningful to the young person, workable within their circumstances and acceptable in their social and emotional context.
Methods: A targeted qualitative content analysis with iterative framework development used data from INcreasing AdolesCent social and community supporT (INACT), a school-based social prescribing programme for pupils experiencing loneliness or low community connection. 38 interviews were screened (12 young people, eight parents/guardians, five school staff and 13 link workers); 37 contained physical-activity material. These were analysed alongside link-worker records for 163 young people. Material was charted by activity category, setting, pathway stage, barriers and inclusion or emotional-safety considerations, then compared across pilot interviews, full-trial interviews and logs. Three researchers contributed to coding, checking and collective interpretation.
Results: Across interviews and routine records, physical-activity material encompassed organised sport, fitness and exercise, dance and creative movement, outdoor activity, informal movement or active recreation, and other community activities. Five overlapping areas of work were identified: understanding interests and personal fit; expanding activity options; supporting access and entry; working through practical feasibility and sustainability; and considering inclusion and emotional safety. These areas were not sequential and could overlap or be revisited. School settings interacted with family routines, peer cultures and community provision to shape usability. Logs more often documented named activities, practical actions and spending, whereas interviews provided fuller accounts of confidence, social fit and family constraints. Pathway stages from discussion and referral to attendance and continuation were not consistently distinguished.
Conclusion: For pupils experiencing loneliness or low community connection, access to a potentially connecting physical activity depended on more than availability or referral. The framework describes the practical, relational and contextual work involved in moving towards meaningful, workable and acceptable participation. It locates responsibility across families, schools, providers, services and local infrastructure while keeping young people’s preferences and choices central. The study does not establish that physical activity reduced loneliness, but provides a basis for prospective evaluation of participation, social connection and loneliness outcomes.

articles_hidden.title: Maternal Anxiety and Depression, Parenting, and Child Social-Emotional Functioning as an Interconnected System: Network Evidence from Born in Bradford
articles_hidden.authors: Bradford Mental Health Research Centre BMHRC; Emre Deniz; Eleanor Jane Bryant; Paul Sullivan; Cara E Staniforth; Reena Uddin; Paul Tiffin; Ruth Wadman
articles_hidden.abstract: Maternal emotional wellbeing and children’s social emotional functioning are closely related. Parenting may play an important role in this relationship, as mothers and children respond to one another’s emotions and behaviours in everyday family life. However, we know less about which specific maternal emotional symptoms, parenting characteristics, and child social-emotional functioning are interconnected within a broader family emotional system. We explored these relationships in 5,143 mother-child dyads from Born in Bradford, a large, ethnically diverse cohort in the United Kingdom. Children were approximately 9 years old and mothers approximately 38 years old. Using cross-sectional psychometric network analysis, we examined the structure connecting maternal depressive and anxiety symptoms, parenting characteristics (e.g., efficacy, affection and strictness), and five domains of children’s social-emotional functioning (i.e., emotional difficulties, peer problems, conduct problems, hyperactivity/impulsivity, and prosocial behaviours). Four distinct but interconnected communities emerged, representing maternal depression, maternal anxiety, parenting, and child social-emotional functioning. Maternal worry-related anxiety symptoms and difficulty relaxing were particularly strongly connected within the overall network, while conduct problems were the most strongly connected child domain. Parenting characteristics, particularly strict parenting, were prominent in connecting maternal and child domains. Together, our findings highlight the value of understanding maternal symptoms, parenting, and child functioning within a broader family emotional system. We propose that interventions may be most effective when they address these two areas together, for example by supporting parental worry and child conduct problems within a shared family-focused approach.

articles_hidden.title: Tones, Dots and Attentional Biases: An autobiographical account of the development, first implementation, and reception of my attentional-probe paradigm (aka dot-probe paradigm)
articles_hidden.authors: Christos Halkiopoulos
articles_hidden.abstract: The attentional probe paradigm involves presenting participants with different messages simultaneously through two distinct information channels within the same modality. By measuring reaction times to modality-specific probes that can appear in either channel, this paradigm enables the assessment of attention allocation between these channels. Since the 1980s this paradigm has become prominent for investigating attentional biases in the processing of emotional information. The best-known version of it, the dot-probe technique introduced by MacLeod, Mathews, and Tata (1986), uses the visual modality. What is less well-known is that I had previously introduced the attentional probe paradigm in 1981 in the auditory modality in a modified dichotic listening experiment with pure tones as auditory probes. Using this tone-probe technique this study investigated the contrasting ways in which repressors and sensitisers (Byrne,1961) handle threatening information. Criticisms from a contemporary perspective notwithstanding of the rather limited initial study, it was concluded that sensitisers displayed an attentional bias favouring the processing of threatening stimuli, whereas repressors appeared to avoid the optimal processing of such stimuli.  This paper presents a historical reconstruction of how I developed the attentional probe paradigm, how I first applied it in the auditory modality, and how it was subsequently used in the visual modality. It also introduces a multimodal version to be used in further research and offers a critique of extant research relying exclusively on decontextualized stimuli.

articles_hidden.title: Bounded and Unbounded Number Line Estimation in Adults: Accuracy, Response Characteristics, and Mathematical Achievement
articles_hidden.authors: Felix Ayesu; Sharon Henry Yakusi; Valentine Ampah
articles_hidden.abstract:
Number line estimation is widely used to examine numerical magnitude processing and its relationship with mathematics. However,
it remains unclear whether mathematical achievement is more closely associated with estimation accuracy or with characteristics of
estimation responses. The present study examined these relationships among 192 adults who completed bounded and unbounded
number line estimation tasks and mathematics assessments covering arithmetic, fractions, algebra, and percentages. Linear,
logarithmic, mixed log-linear, proportional judgment, and scallop models were compared to characterize estimation responses. We
also evaluated the relationships of estimation accuracy and fitted-response characteristics with mathematical achievement. Linear
models best predicted bounded estimation, whereas mixed log-linear and selected scallop models offered small improvements
for unbounded estimation. Greater linearity and stronger proportional judgment model fit were associated with greater bounded
estimation accuracy, while mixed log-linear characteristics were related to estimation error in both tasks. Bounded estimation accuracy
was more consistently associated with mathematical achievement than unbounded accuracy. Most fitted-response characteristics
accounted for little additional variation in mathematics after considering estimation accuracy, although exploratory analyses indicated
that mixed-model characteristics contributed modest additional information. The findings highlight the value of distinguishing
estimation accuracy from the mathematical characteristics of estimation responses when investigating individual differences in
mathematical achievement.

articles_hidden.title: Post-Encoding Semantic Processing Produces Systematic Distortions in Episodic Memory
articles_hidden.authors: Katelyn G. Cliver; Kennedy N King; Alexa Tompary
