articles_hidden.abstract: How new experiences can update a memory has important consequences for its long-term storage, but little is known about how different kinds of re exposure may differentially influence its content. Inspired by theories of memory reconstruction that posit that memory retrieval depends on the integration of idiosyncratic details and relevant general knowledge, we investigated how exposure to a memory through category- or item-level processing may strengthen its episodic and semantic components. Across three behavioral experiments, participants encoded image-location associations in a protocol designed to generate a conflict between memory for specific images and knowledge of the general location of other images from the same category. Following learning of the locations, participants completed manipulations aimed to prioritize category-level or item-level processing of the images. We hypothesized that requiring semantic processing after learning would reinforce prior category knowledge associated with each image and increase category-driven distortions in memory at test. Our findings revealed that memory for images that underwent semantic processing were less precise and more distorted relative to memories that underwent item-level processing and relative to those that were not re-exposed after encoding. Furthermore, post-encoding manipulations more strongly updated memories of atypical category members, suggesting that the organization of prior knowledge can govern the extent that new memories can be updated. Together, these results highlight the active role of post‑encoding manipulations in differentially reshaping memory content and provide compelling evidence that episodic memory retrieval is a constructive process that integrates across prior knowledge, discrete experiences, and subsequent re-exposure.

articles_hidden.title: Does the Variance of Personality Traits Change Across the Lifespan? A Meta-Analytic Review of Longitudinal Studies
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Haehner; Susanne Buecker; Marco Altorfer; Vera Bocklet; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles_hidden.abstract: Although personality traits are relatively stable compared to other constructs, comprehensive meta-analyses have shown that the mean-levels and rank-orders of personality traits change throughout the lifespan. In contrast, relatively little is known about whether and how the variance of personality traits develops with age. Examining changes in personality trait variance is, however, critical to contextualize knowledge on mean-level changes, to identify disruptive life phases, to evaluate the changes in predictive utility of personality traits, and to advance personality development theories. The present meta-analysis thus integrated research from 362 longitudinal studies (Ntotal = 398,124) to identify changes in personality trait variance across time and age. We found remarkable stability of personality variance for all traits, indicating that, at the population level, people neither get more different nor more alike across the lifespan. The only deviations from this pattern were variance increases in neuroticism during late childhood and early adolescence (5 to 14 years) and variance decreases in extraversion during middle and late adulthood (45 to 80 years). Notably, though, effect sizes differed substantially across studies and measures. Our results provide novel insights into the lifespan development of personality traits that can be used to advance theoretical frameworks and inform practical applications. Furthermore, by providing benchmark values for the comparison of effect size estimates of future studies (https://personalityresearch.shinyapps.io/VarianceChange/), we aim to facilitate more systematic and cumulative research on variance changes in psychological traits.

articles_hidden.title: Validating the Big Five Aspect Scales (BFAS) and the Short Form (BFAS-40) in German, French, and Italian
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Haehner; Michael Dominik Krämer; Wiebke Bleidorn; Christopher James Hopwood
articles_hidden.abstract: Personality traits predict health, well-being, relationship success, and work-related outcomes, but most of the relevant evidence comes from English-speaking populations. The Big Five Aspect Scales (BFAS) are one of the most used English-language personality questionnaires, allowing to assess Big Five domains and aspects validly and reliably. In the present study, we validated German, French, and Italian translations of the BFAS and its short-form (BFAS-40) in a representative sample of Swiss adults (N = 4,492). Across the three languages, the translations of the BFAS and the BFAS-40 showed satisfactory psychometric properties in terms of their factorial validity, reliability, and convergence of short- and long-version. Furthermore, we found partial weak measurement invariance across the three languages for all aspects and domains and strong invariance for some aspects. Finally, in line with existing research, aspects belonging to the same Big Five domain differed in their associations with external variables like political orientation and life satisfaction. The translations of the BFAS and the BFAS-40 may thus facilitate future research on personality traits in non-English speaking samples.

articles_hidden.title: Human similarity judgments reveal fine-grained representations of dynamic social scenes
articles_hidden.authors: Kathy Garcia; Leyla Isik
articles_hidden.abstract: How does the human mind organize dynamic social scenes? Existing accounts rely on pre-defined social-affective or action-based taxonomies, yet whether humans use these dimensions to structure their representations of naturalistic social scenes remains unknown. We collected 53,223 human similarity judgments of videos depicting two-person actions and trained a sparse-positive-embedding model to recover the underlying latent dimensions. These learned dimensions explained twice as much variance in similarity judgments as pre-labeled annotations, captured interpretable fine-grained social-event structure (combining information about social relationships and actions), and fractionated broad semantic content (e.g., separating parent-child interactions into caregiving versus affectionate play). The same dimensions also predicted fMRI responses to passively viewed stimuli across visual cortex better than pre-labeled annotations, highlighting their importance beyond similarity judgments. Together, these results suggest that humans represent dynamic social scenes along fine-grained axes not captured by current taxonomies, and offer behaviorally-grounded targets for future studies of social vision.

articles_hidden.title: A Systematic Review and Theoretical Framework of Stress Generation in Daily Life
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Haehner; Rosalie Andrae; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles_hidden.abstract: Stress generation describes processes by which individuals actively contribute to the occurrence of self-generated stressful events. Personal characteristics like neuroticism or psychopathology have been found to predict the occurrence of major life stressors over several months or years. However, a profound understanding of stress generation over shorter time periods in people’s daily lives is still missing. Here, we integrated recent research on person-environment transactions from personality psychology into the clinical stress generation literature to develop a process model of stress generation. This process model posits that stress generation unfolds across multiple timescales and that short-term dynamics between momentary, state-level personal characteristics and daily hassles are the building blocks for established long-term stress generation effects. To evaluate a core aspect of this model, we conducted a systematic literature search on stress generation in daily life (45 studies, Ntotal = 9’818). Results show that both dispositional traits and momentary states predict the occurrence of daily hassles, supporting the existence and relevance of stress generation in daily life. However, future research on stress generation across timescales is needed to test the theorized link between stress generation in daily life and long-term stress generation effects.

articles_hidden.title: A Smartphone-Based Intervention to Decrease Neuroticism: Protocol of the CHILL Study
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Haehner; Amanda Jo Wright; Rosalie Andrae; Till Lubczyk; Leyla Anina Rosero Betancourt§; Christopher James Hopwood; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles_hidden.abstract: Many people worldwide want to be less neurotic. As lower levels of neuroticism predict a range of positive life outcomes, including health, work success, and relationship quality, interventions that help people to become less neurotic could have wide ranging impacts. This study protocol describes the rationale and design of the CHILL Study (Changing How I Live Life) that aims to evaluate the effects of a smartphone-based intervention to reduce neuroticism in the general public. The CHILL Study comprises four survey assessments spread over 5 months, a 6-week intervention phase, and two 1-week experience sampling phases without interventions. During the intervention phase, participants who wanted to become less neurotic were randomized to four different treatment groups. These treatment groups differed in the employed intervention strategies that target different aspects and levels of neuroticism. The CHILL Study moves beyond existing research on volitional personality change by testing which strategies most effectively decrease neuroticism and evaluating the longevity and generalizability of intervention-induced neuroticism change via peer-reports, implicit personality assessments, and a 7-week follow-up period. The goals of the CHILL Study are to generate an effective method for decreasing neuroticism and facilitating the development of a comprehensive theory of neuroticism change.

articles_hidden.title: Personality Predictors of Health, Well-Being, Relationships, and Employment in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa: A Three-Year Longitudinal Study
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Haehner; Catherine Mkaleso Shirima; Marie-Christin Kura; Luzelle Naude; Christopher James Hopwood; Amber Gayle Thalmayer
articles_hidden.abstract: Personality traits have been found to be robust predictors of important life outcomes. However, evidence on longitudinal personality-outcome associations stems almost exclusively from Western countries. It is not yet known if, how, and to what extent personality traits are robustly linked to life outcomes in sub-Saharan Africa. Using data from the Africa Long Life Study, which sampled young adults from Kenya, Namibia, and South Africa (N = 2,770), we examined the Big Two personality traits, agency and communion, as predictors of seven life outcomes (self-reported health, life satisfaction, depression, anxiety, employment status, relationship status, financial situation) 2 to 3 years later. We used specification curve analysis to examine the robustness of personality-outcome associations. Higher levels of agency and communion robustly predicted higher levels of self-rated health and lower levels of anxiety and depression over 2 to 3 years. Furthermore, higher levels of communion predicted being employed 2 to 3 years later. However, personality-outcome associations were smaller than previously observed in Western countries (.02 ≤ |r| ≤ .11) and depended on analytic decisions such as country and the time lag between assessments. Our findings provide novel insights into the cross-cultural replicability of personality-outcome associations.

articles_hidden.title: Ten Concerns About Personality-Change Interventions—and How to Address Them
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Haehner; Eva Asselmann; Saskia Baumgardt; Lena Brüggmann; Jaap J. A. Denissen; Claudia Harzer; Christina M. Juchem; Michael Dominik Krämer; Niclas Kuper; Lara Puhlmann
articles_hidden.abstract: Many people want to change their personality in some way and personality traits have been found to predict various important aspects of life, including well-being, health, relationship quality, and work success. As a result, volitional personality interventions designed to elicit personality trait change in desired directions have recently gained momentum in research and public discourse. Although the initial evidence on the effectiveness of these interventions is promising, concerns regarding their benefits, risks, and societal implications remain underexplored. In this review, we discuss 10 concerns regarding methodological, ethical, and practical limitations of volitional personality change interventions. Drawing on research across different areas of psychology, we provide a balanced discussion of each concern and outline directions for future research and practical applications of these interventions. Volitional personality change interventions have the potential to improve people’s life and increase satisfaction with the self. However, realizing this potential requires sustained research efforts, thoughtful study design, and careful implementation of these interventions to maximize benefits and mitigate concerns.

articles_hidden.title: Individual Differences in Personality Trait Changes Across the Lifespan: A Meta-Analysis of Longitudinal Studies
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Haehner; Christopher James Hopwood; Lukas Schellenberg; Ted Schwaba; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent meta-analyses and large-scale longitudinal studies have shown that the mean-levels and rank-orders of personality traits change throughout the lifespan. However, people differ from each other in their patterns of personality development. These individual differences in personality trait changes provide important insight into the sources and course of personality development. The present meta-analysis quantified the magnitude of individual differences in personality trait changes and their fluctuation across time lags and age by integrating findings from 229 longitudinal studies (N = 230,492). Results indicated significant individual differences in change in all traits, with neuroticism showing the most pronounced differences, and openness and agreeableness the least. Charting effects across the lifespan, individual differences in change were most pronounced in childhood, decreased during young adulthood, but were significant across the entire lifespan. The age at which individual differences in change were smallest varied across traits, from ages 30 to 75. Finally, individual differences in personality trait changes were larger over longer assessment intervals, for facet-level traits, and among measures that were not designed to examine the Big Five taxonomy. Our findings support theoretical claims that highlight the relevance of genetic and environmental sources of personality development and suggest that individual differences in change endure, challenging the predictions of set-point models of personality development. Moreover, our results provide benchmarks for individual differences in change that can be used to compare the magnitude of differential personality development in future research.

articles_hidden.title: Questionable mediated effect of self-management on athletic performance: A comment on Fan et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles_hidden.abstract: Drawing on the covariance matrix reported by Fan et al., I reassessed the empirical basis of their mediation model linking self-management to athletic performance. I demonstrate that the observed covariance structure can be reproduced by a theoretically different latent-variable model that does not rely on the directional mechanism proposed in the original article. In this alternative account, self-reported self-management, psychological resilience, competitive spirit, and athletic performance are conceptualized as indicators of a broader construct, core self-evaluation. The results illustrate a broader inferential problem in psychological research: multiple theoretically plausible models may provide equally adequate explanations of the same correlational pattern. Consequently, observational associations alone offer limited grounds for preferring one explanation over competing alternatives. Researchers should therefore routinely evaluate alternative models when drawing inferences about psychological mechanisms from nonexperimental data.

articles_hidden.title: Stress Generation Across Hours, Days, and 1 Month
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Haehner; Lukas Schellenberg; Michael Dominik Krämer; Amanda Jo Wright; Wiebke Bleidorn; Christopher James Hopwood
articles_hidden.abstract: Stressful events can trigger mental health problems. Mental health problems, in turn, predict the occurrence of stressful events—a phenomenon called stress generation, which can initiate detrimental cycles between stress and mental health. However, existing research has focused on long-term stress generation. Here, we aimed to advance the understanding of how stress generation unfolds across different timescales by combing experience sampling, daily diary, and 1-month longitudinal data (N = 403). We found that between-person differences in depression, rumination, reassurance seeking, and neuroticism were linked to the occurrence of daily hassles over hours and days and major life stressors over a month. Furthermore, momentary neuroticism and rumination prospectively predicted the occurrence of daily hassles over several hours. Finally, some indicators of hourly and daily stress generation prospectively predicted the occurrence of major life stressors. These findings provide the starting point for a thorough understanding of how stress generation unfolds over time.

articles_hidden.title: Event-Related Changes in Personality Traits, Life Satisfaction, and Mental Health: Evidence from a 4-Year Longitudinal Study in sub-Saharan Africa
articles_hidden.authors: Peter Haehner; Tracy-Ann Adonis; STEPHEN ASATSA; Maria Florence; Tasneem Hassem; Daniel Hofmann; Christopher James Hopwood; Marie-Christin Kura; Sumaya Laher; Luzelle Naude
articles_hidden.abstract: Life events like entering a romantic relationship or losing a job have been found to predict changes in personality traits and well-being. However, findings on event-related changes stem almost exclusively from Western countries. Here, we address this limitation by examining event-related changes in agency, communion, life satisfaction, and mental health among young adults living in Namibia, Kenya, and South Africa (N = 3,928). A finding that converged with prior meta-analyses from Western contexts was that childbirth predicted decreases in agency whereas event-related changes in other events diverged substantially from findings in Western samples. For example, finishing education or getting a driver’s license predicted decreases in agency and communion. Furthermore, having first sexual intercourse was associated with decreases in mental health. Future cross-cultural research is needed to test potential explanations for why event-related changes differ across cultural contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Working at a Cost? ADHD Symptoms, Self-Endangering Work Behavior, and Occupational Well-Being
articles_hidden.authors: Kerstin Erdal; Johanna Kreft; Johanna Finnemann
articles_hidden.abstract:
Self-endangering work behavior (SEWB) describes strategies employees use to maintain occupational functioning despite potential costs to health and recovery. This study examined associations between attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), SEWB, and occupational well-being using variable- and person-centred approaches.
Participants were 471 working adults in Germany; 176 met the ADHD criterion based on self-reported diagnosis and/or a positive Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale screen. Group differences across ten SEWB dimensions and associations with burnout, work engagement, and perceived stress were examined. Latent profile analysis identified configurations of continuous ADHD symptoms and SEWB.
Participants in the ADHD group reported higher levels across all SEWB dimensions (ds = .20–.78). SEWB dimensions showed differentiated associations with occupational well-being, with little evidence that these associations differed by ADHD group. Four ADHD–SEWB profiles differed across all well-being outcomes but did not reproduce categorical ADHD group membership.
ADHD-related characteristics may represent one person-level correlate of SEWB, while substantial heterogeneity exists in how ADHD symptoms and SEWB co-occur and relate to occupational well-being. Findings should be interpreted considering the cross-sectional design, highly educated sample, and ADHD classification based on self-report and screening.

articles_hidden.title: Age-related changes in strategy use during reinforcement learning
articles_hidden.authors: Irene van de Vijver; Leendert van Maanen
articles_hidden.abstract: Age-related declines in reinforcement learning (RL) are commonly attributed to impairments in dopaminergic prediction-error learning and working memory. However, successful RL may also depend on discovering and applying higher-order learning strategies that reduce memory demands. We investigated whether age differences in RL partly reflect reduced spontaneous strategy discovery, whether providing support attenuates these differences, and whether these effects depend on stimulus verbalizability. Sixty younger and 59 older adults completed an RL task in which stimulus-response mappings either contained no underlying structure or could be grouped according to semantic or visual regularities. Across four phases, participants received increasingly explicit information about these regularities. Strategy use was assessed using verbal reports and by fitting sigmoid functions to individual learning curves, estimating the transition to strategy-based responding. Older adults showed lower learning performance, reported using strategies less frequently, and transitioned later to strategy-based responding than younger adults. Providing structured stimulus-response mappings and increasingly explicit information improved learning performance, increased reported strategy use, and accelerated strategy discovery in both age groups, with the largest performance gains observed in older adults and for concrete compared to abstract stimuli. Verbal fluency predicted both learning performance and strategy discovery. These findings suggest that age-related differences in RL reflect not only declines in associative learning but also reduced spontaneous discovery and application of effective learning strategies. Facilitating strategy discovery may therefore represent a promising way to improve learning in older adulthood.

articles_hidden.title: Conspiratorial echoes of disease: The relationship between pathogen prevalence and conspiracy beliefs
articles_hidden.authors: Maciej Siemiątkowski; Maciej Górski; Michał Bilewicz; Theofilos Gkinopoulos; Brian W. Haas; NA; Mohsen Joshanloo; Paul Shing-fong Chan; Ari Nowacki; Efisio Manunta
articles_hidden.abstract: Conspiracy beliefs vary substantially across countries and regions, yet the ecological factors underlying this variation remain largely unexplored. Drawing on behavioral immune system theory, which suggests that pathogen threat can heighten vigilance toward potential dangers, we examined whether pathogen prevalence predicts conspiracy beliefs. Study 1 analyzed four cross-national datasets (20-32 countries) and found that conspiracy beliefs were higher in countries with greater historical pathogen prevalence. Study 2 tested this relationship in a preregistered study using a larger sample (N = 15,503 from 55 countries) and found that historical pathogen prevalence predicted higher levels of conspiracy beliefs. Study 3 extended these findings to the US state level using data from 123,781 participants across 50 states. Finally, Study 4 (N = 493) experimentally manipulated perceived pathogen prevalence and found causal effects on generic and vaccine-related conspiracy beliefs. These findings extend behavioral immune system research by relating pathogen-rich ecologies to contemporary conspiracy thinking.

articles_hidden.title: Urban Aesthetics: Beauty and Interestingness of the City
articles_hidden.authors: Joerg Fingerhut
articles_hidden.abstract:
This paper develops an empirically informed aesthetics of the city by introducing interestingness as a
complementary category to beauty. While beauty has long defined architectural value through
harmony and rightness, urban life also requires experiences of dissonance, openness, and surprise.
Contrasting Scruton’s notion of architectural beauty with Mumford’s conception of the city as secular
and dramatic, I side with Mumford’s more open understanding of urban life.

Conceptually, I propose a middle way that neither centers exclusively on beauty nor simply endorses
a pluralist aesthetics of the city, as is common in contemporary philosophy of the city. To capture the
psychology of urban life, I focus on aesthetic emotions that help explain the experiences of beauty,
interestingness, and belonging. Methodologically, I likewise argue for a middle way that combines
philosophical reflection with empirical research on the psychology and neuroscience of the built
environment. Taken together, the paper outlines an urban-theoretical framework that understands
urban public space, in particular, as an aesthetic interface linking perception, affect, and cognition to
forms of civic participation. Beauty provides coherence; interestingness sustains vitality. Together,
they define the aesthetic and psychological livability of the city.

Keywords
Aesthetic emotions; Affordances; Beauty; Empirical aesthetics; Interestingness; Neurourbanism,
Urban Aesthetics

articles_hidden.title: Speech Monitoring During Self-Comprehension
articles_hidden.authors: Andreas Lind; Petter Johansson; Lars Hall
articles_hidden.abstract: Spontaneous speech is full of false starts, rephrasing, and speech errors. Speakers’ ability to detect errors and other problems in their own speech is commonly explained by monitoring mechanisms that rely on pre-articulatory representations, production states, or derivative predictions. We develop an alternative, cue-integrative account in which verbal self-monitoring is a natural consequence of what we have previously termed self-comprehension: speakers’ integration of contextual and sensory information to understand their own unfolding speech without requiring that meaning or intention be fully specified before articulation. Two sources of anticipatory information are central to the account, neither requiring explicit predictive or forward-model representations. First, we apply to self-comprehension the recently proposed idea of multi-scale pattern completion during speech comprehension, which allows partial input to activate continuations at multiple linguistic levels, generating contextually constrained anticipation. Second, anticipatory coarticulation can provide auditory and somatosensory information about upcoming speech before the relevant segment is produced, challenging the assumption that sensory feedback is too slow for online self-comprehension. We propose three routes to error detection: divergence between pattern-completion-based and coarticulatory anticipations; divergence between pattern-completion-based anticipation and post-articulatory sensory feedback; and post-articulatory self-comprehension in the absence of sufficiently informative anticipation. These routes provide a framework for explaining error detection across the observed range of error-interruption latencies, including very rapid interruptions. This framework also provides alternative interpretations of error-detection findings under noise-masked auditory feedback and of cortical attenuation during speaking without requiring a separate pre-articulatory monitoring channel, explicit predictions, or prediction-error computations.

articles_hidden.title: Culturally embedded affect: A grounded theory of recursive eco-emotional processing in young adults in Nepal and India
articles_hidden.authors: Samridha S J B Rana; Paul Graham Morris; Emily-Marie Pacheco
articles_hidden.abstract:
The climate and ecological crises disproportionately affect communities from low-and-middle-income-countries, yet to date most studies of eco-emotions have been with Western populations. This study sought to investigate the views and experiences of young adults in Nepal and India regarding emotional responses and coping to the ecological and climate crises. 

Using constructivist grounded theory, interviews were conducted with twenty-four young adults, equally split between region (Delhi national-capital-region in India, and Kathmandu Valley in Nepal); poor and middle-class urban populations; and male/female sex, to ensure a suitable range of experiences. 

The grounded theory model proposes that eco-emotional experiences are initiated by lived ecological disruption, such as air pollution, heat, and environmental degradation, rather than via abstract knowledge of climate change. These disruptions are then interpreted through culturally embedded meaning systems, including religious practices, agricultural rhythms, and place-based identity, and are further shaped by structural inequalities, such as socioeconomic positioning and perceived political inaction. 

Eco-emotions emerge not as discrete states but as dynamic configurations, in which anxiety, anger, sadness, grief, hope, and helplessness coexist and fluctuate. Perceived agency operates as a key interpretive dimension influencing emotional trajectories. Where agency is experienced as viable, distress may be channelled into problem-focussed or meaning-focussed coping. Where agency is constrained, coping shifts towards strategies that regulate distress through psychological distancing, including fatalism, resignation, and disengagement. Coping processes recursively reshape how ecological disruptions are interpreted over time. 

This framework situates eco-emotions within the intersection of ecological change, cultural meaning-making, and structural inequality, offering a contextually grounded account of their emergence and regulation.

articles_hidden.title: “If you don’t vape, it’s abnormal”: Attitudes, perspectives, and perceived functions of vaping and nicotine pouches in Ireland
articles_hidden.authors: Rory Coyne; Cheyenne Downey; Mengyang Zhang; Gintare Valentelyte; Paul Kavanagh; Jan Sørensen; Frank Doyle
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction: Increasing usage of novel nicotine products, including e-cigarettes/vapes and oral nicotine pouches risks proliferating long-term nicotine addiction and adverse health consequences among a new generation. Public health responses are evolving, but need to be informed by a deep understanding of complex and emerging behaviours. While previous research has explored patterns of vaping and nicotine use, less is known about their perceived functions and social meanings. The present study sought to explore attitudes and perceptions of vaping and nicotine pouch use, and the perceived functions that they have among users. 
Methods: This study employed an exploratory, qualitative design, adopting an epistemological stance of social constructionism. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with users of vapes and nicotine pouches aged ≥16 years in Ireland. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. An analytic structure with five themes was generated.
Results: Participants described vaping as a means of managing stress and anxiety, framing vaping particularly as a coping strategy. Nicotine more broadly was constructed as a lifestyle or wellness supplement which supported concentration and productivity. Despite widespread perceived normalisation, participants described feeling ashamed of being a nicotine user. 
Conclusion: These findings show that participants continue to vape and use nicotine pouches not only because of dependency, but also due to perceived emotional, cognitive and lifestyle functions attributed to nicotine. Prevention and cessation efforts are therefore likely to benefit from addressing the perceived functions of vaping and nicotine pouch use, whilst challenging misconceptions surrounding the benefits of nicotine and avoiding stigma associated with nicotine dependency.

articles_hidden.title: Do people believe diet impacts physical and mental health? Development and validation of the Diet-Health Belief Scale (DHBS)
articles_hidden.authors: Jane Brealey; Joanna Brooks; Zoé Colombet; Rebecca Evans; Eric Robinson
articles_hidden.abstract: Diet can impact on physical and mental health, but to what extent do people believe this? Health psychology theory proposes that beliefs about the impact diet has on health likely shape behaviour. Yet, diet-health beliefs have not been systematically studied and methodology used in existing research is limited. This two-part study aimed to explore UK adults’ beliefs about the impact diet has on short-term and long-term physical and mental health conditions, and to conduct initial development and validation of a scale to measure diet-health beliefs. An initial 20-item scale was completed by a general population sample of 399 UK adults online. Results show that participants had inconsistent beliefs about the impact diet has on long-term and short-term physical health outcomes. Participants tended not to believe that diet impacts mental health. Next, exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis of survey responses indicated a 15-item two factor (physical health, mental health) scale provided the most statistically appropriate measure of diet-health beliefs. The scale was found to be reliable at both full (ωₜ = 0.93) and subscale level (factor 1: physical health, ωₜ = 0.90, factor 2: mental health, ωₜ = 0.93). Convergent, divergent and test-retest validity assessments confirmed the scale had acceptable validity. The scale could be used to investigate whether beliefs about the impact of diet on health shape dietary behaviour and investigate the effectiveness of interventions designed to change diet-health beliefs.

articles_hidden.title: Understanding what works in school food policy: A multistakeholder approach to quantify policy
articles_hidden.authors: Katie Leigh Edwards; Sarah Newton; Jacqueline Blissett; Suzanne Higgs
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Most children do not meet nutrition recommendations. Primary schools are a key setting for improving children’s healthy eating, yet overlapping policy guidance can make it difficult for schools to determine which food policies to adopt. Research is needed to quantify which policy components are most effective, feasible, and tailorable to school and child needs, and to identify the mechanisms through which they influence behaviour.
Methods: A multistakeholder approach was taken: 1) consultation with food policy experts to provide insights and feedback about the project; 2) scoping of policies across England and Wales to identify effective policy components and the potential mechanisms by which policies may be working to improve healthy eating; 3) engagement sessions with stakeholders (school staff) and end-users (children) in primary schools in Birmingham, UK; and 4) triangulation of insights gained. Fourteen individual policy components were identified. Each component was quantified using indicators of effectiveness (expert opinion; empirical evidence), feasibility (child endorsement; staff views; financial and resource demands), and opportunity for tailoring. Theoretical mechanisms were mapped to each policy component to demonstrate core pathways. 
Results: Scores varied across components. ‘Learning about food’, ‘role modelling’, and ‘eating with others’ ranked highest across indicators, while components such as ‘growing food’ and ‘preparation or cooking food’ were limited by cost and resource demands. Five components had limited or no empirical evidence despite perceived feasibility. Twelve components were rated as having moderate to high potential for tailoring to school and child needs. Six mechanisms were identified (exposure, food accessibility, motivation, social influences, and knowledge- and skills-based food literacy), each mapping onto multiple policy components. 
Conclusion: This study provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the effectiveness, feasibility, and opportunity for tailoring school food policy components, alongside the mechanisms through which they may operate. Findings offer practical guidance to support schools and policymakers in selecting and tailoring policies to diverse contexts. Further research should test the proposed mechanisms and explore how tailored approaches can improve healthy eating for all children.

articles_hidden.title: Racial resentment continues to characterize White Americans’ support for Donald Trump
articles_hidden.authors: David Michael Amodio; Jeffrey Jordan Berg; Lee Q. Cui; Andreas Schuck; Anke Stoll; Madalina Vlasceanu
articles_hidden.abstract: Despite the popular narrative that White Americans supported Donald Trump in 2016 due to economic concerns, several studies show that their support is more strongly predicted by a variety of social issues concerning race and gender. The present work sought to characterize the core features of these social issues among White Americans by assessing 15 self-report and behavioral measures of social attitudes, in addition to several economic, political, and demographic indicators, and comparing their relative effects on Trump support during the Biden and second Trump presidential terms. In both studies, conducted in 2022 (N=906) and 2026 (N=1206), racial resentment was the strongest predictor of Trump support relative to all other measures of social, economic, and political concerns. Economic stress was negatively associated with Trump support. Furthermore, we find that, among conservatives, the relation between racial resentment and Trump support aligns more closely with MAGA identity than with conservatism generally. These findings clarify the nature of White Americans’ support for Trump, show its sustained association across presidential administrations, and link it closely to the MAGA movement.

articles_hidden.title: Contextual modulations at low and high levels of visual perception: functional (in)dependence and influence of local contrast
articles_hidden.authors: Mehmet Umut Canoluk; Marius Grandjean; Valerie Goffaux
articles_hidden.abstract: What we see depends on context. From low to high levels of the visual system hierarchy, the amplitude of contextual influences is a function of local input strength. In the case of human face perception, the influence exerted by face context on local feature discrimination is determined by that feature discriminability. Face contextual modulations are presumed to rely on high-level, specialized contextual mechanisms, with little contribution of low-level mechanisms. The shared dependence of low- and high-level contextual modulations on local input strength however suggests they may be linked functionally. The present registered report addresses this gap by investigating whether consistent individual differences exist in contextual modulations across low-level contrast detection and high-level facial feature discrimination. Across tasks, we manipulated the contrast (i.e., strength) of a local input target (local grating and eye region, respectively) presented either in isolation or embedded in context. The context in the contrast detection task refers to a larger surrounding grating while it refers to the facial features surrounding the target eye region in the facial feature discrimination task. The comparison of contrast thresholds across conditions provided a metric to evaluate contextual modulation magnitudes. For both upright feature discrimination and contrast detection, context exerted a strong suppressive influence on local target processing; i.e., incongruent face context and parallel surround increased contrast threshold for feature discrimination and grating detection, respectively, compared to isolated viewing condition. As expected, face inversion drastically reduced the influence of context on local contrast threshold. We found no conclusive proof of a functional link between the magnitude of contextual modulation in local contrast detection and face feature matching; there was however extreme evidence for the correlation of contextual modulation magnitude in upright and inverted face feature matching. By investigating the shared variance between the contextual modulation magnitudes across visual processing levels, this study aimed at a system-wide understanding of the influence of spatial context on vision. Despite low- and high-level contextual modulations sharing similar operating principles, the present findings suggest they may involve independent mechanisms. We outline methodological approaches for further research development on this topic.

articles_hidden.title: Mothers’ Abuse Reports Under Uncertainty: Why Custody Courts’ Default Response Fails the Child
articles_hidden.authors: Vera Wilde
articles_hidden.abstract: When mothers report that a father is abusing them or their children, family courts in many countries respond with suspicion of the mother: the report is recast as evidence that she is alienating the child, and custody sometimes moves to the accused father. Two literatures bear on this response. One shows that unsubstantiated reports are routinely treated as false, although intentional fabrication is uncommon and, in custody disputes, comes more often from noncustodial parents than from custodial mothers. The other shows that credibility judgments based on demeanor perform near chance and follow observers’ expectations of how a victim should appear, so that a distressed mother and a composed mother can each be disbelieved. We argue that the alienation inference, as commonly applied, is confirmatory hypothesis testing: the report itself, the mother’s worry and her compliance are all counted in its favor, so nothing can count against it. We then model the court’s choice as a decision under uncertainty, with several risk pathways and at least three actions. Provided that supervision reduces the child’s exposure to risks running through the accused parent and that separation from the primary caregiver does more harm than the burden of supervision, keeping the child with the primary caregiver under supervised contact dominates transfer to the accused parent for any probability of abuse; transfer can be preferred only on independent evidence that the mother herself endangers the child, at a threshold that rises with the risk posed by the father. We explain why these errors persist unmeasured, review legal reforms in Spain, Italy, England and Wales, and Germany, and propose procedural safeguards and outcome tracking.

articles_hidden.title: Conventionality and transparency in human language
articles_hidden.authors: Sihan Chen; Antonio Benítez-Burraco
articles_hidden.abstract:
The most distinctive feature of language is perhaps the ability to produce and comprehend utterances
that have never been said before. This requires language to be transparent: comprehenders
can infer the meaning of an utterance based on its components and the rules used to combine them.
However, arbitrary associations between form and meaning (conventionality) are ubiquitous in language,
despite them being difficult to learn. This is true for words, but also for many utterances.
Why is this the case? In this paper, we propose languages balance conventionality and transparency
by minimizing the communication and learning cost. While transparency facilitates learnability and
comprehensibility, encoding every meaning transparently inevitably results in longer words, which
raises the communication cost. On the other hand, conventionality enables meanings to be encoded
arbitrarily, allowing more frequent meanings to have shorter words, which minimizes the communication
cost, but it also makes words and utterances more opaque, thus increasing understanding and
learning cost. We hypothesized that more frequent words are more likely to be conventionalized.
We also hypothesized communities with a higher degree of shared exposure to the common ground
tend to have a higher proportion of conventionalized words. First, we conducted a cost-minimizing
simulation, and the results supported both hypotheses. Then, we empirically tested the first hypothesis,
using a novel metric on semantic transparency, and we found support to it, since more frequent
words in English are indeed less semantically transparent. Overall, our findings support a trade-off
between conventionality and transparency in human languages.

articles_hidden.title: Non-medical use of nitrous oxide – a systematic review of motivational drives
articles_hidden.authors: Anna E. Schütze; Klara Greisiger; Thomas Günther Riemer; Lukas A. Basedow
articles_hidden.abstract:
Introduction: Nitrous oxide (N2O) is a psychoactive substance with euphoric and mildly hallucinogenic effects and a variety of medical applications. Non-medical use of N2O is widespread and in recent years, there has been a significant increase across the world. To investigate potential drivers of this increase, this review summarizes the current state of research on use motives for N2O use.
Methods: A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, PubPsych, PsycInfo, and PsycArticles including quantitative and qualitative reports published up to March 28th, 2026. Qualitative reports were coded according to the five-factor model of substance use motives assigning material to the dimensions of enhancement, coping, expansion, conformity, social and other motives. 
Results: A total of 50 articles were included. Three survey studies were identified that reported enhancement as the major motivational drive. In contrast, the qualitative reports contained coping motives as the most prominent drive. Enhancement and expansion motives were also reported, while social and conformity motives were nearly absent from the qualitative literature. 
Discussion: The non-medical use of N2O is related to a diverse array of motivational forces, with enhancement and coping with negative psychological and physical sensations appearing to be particularly relevant. Recreational non-problematic use seems to be dominated by enhancement motives, while escalated and use with adverse consequences is more strongly related to coping motives. As systematic assessments with validated instruments regarding the motivational drives behind N2O use are lacking, further research is needed to make reliable statements about the motive profile of N2O.

articles_hidden.title: Examining Linking Language and Causal Implications in Observational Psychological Capital Research
articles_hidden.authors: Elise Mockett; Matt N Williams; Dianne Gardner; Larry Paing
articles_hidden.abstract: The present study examines whether the issues with implied causal inference identified by Haber et al. (2022) in observational health research extend to the field of industrial-organisational (IO) psychology. Haber et al. found that causal relationships were implied through the language used to link exposures and outcomes and through recommendations for action. This small-scale conceptual replication applies Haber et al.’s approach to psychological capital (PsyCap), an increasingly popular construct in the domain of IO psychology. Specifically, we evaluate the causal strength of the language used to describe the nature of the connection between given variables when reporting findings and when making recommendations for action in 50 PsyCap articles. The majority of action recommendations were found to have strong causal implications (85% in abstracts, 84% in discussion sections), and most linking sentences implied some level of causality (64% in abstracts, 58% in discussion sections). This was despite very few articles explicitly stating an intention to estimate causal effects (10%) and many explicitly warning against drawing causal inferences (42%). No significant relationship was found between the causality implied in the linking sentences and the strength of causal implication of the action recommendations. These findings have important implications for how research is implemented, and very real consequences for those who are the focus of such implementations. Increased transparency about causal interests and reasoning is needed to uphold the credibility of findings and the integrity of applications of observational PsyCap research.

articles_hidden.title: Subjective and mobile EEG responses to wood-clad and drywall interior environments: An in situ crossover study
articles_hidden.authors: Julianna Marie Mollica; Analia Marzoratti; Tanya Evans; Jennifer Roe; Panos Mavros
articles_hidden.abstract: Exposure to natural environments has been associated with benefits for health and wellbeing, and natural materials offer one avenue for introducing nature-associated elements into interiors. However, relatively little in situ research has examined subjective and neural responses to full-scale interiors with contrasting material characteristics. In this within-subject crossover study, 36 students completed 10-min immersions in wood-clad and white drywall prototype pods following a mental arithmetic task while self-report data and mobile electroencephalography (EEG) were collected. Adjusted models indicated greater momentary nature connectedness and perceived restorative qualities in the wood-clad pod, as well as higher hedonic tone and energetic arousal and lower stress. The primary frontal EEG measures did not differ significantly between pods after correction for multiple comparisons. Together, these findings show that contrasting full-scale interiors elicited distinct immediate subjective responses without corresponding robust differences in selected frontal EEG measures, highlighting the value of multimodal in situ approaches for studying architectural experience.

articles_hidden.title: CortexLens: Systematically Decoding Interpretable Visual Patterns from Human Visual Cortex
articles_hidden.authors: Qinglin Qi; Yiming Tang; Lu Mi; Juan Zhou; Zhenguang Garry Cai; Xufeng Duan; Dianbo Liu
articles_hidden.abstract: Understanding how the human brain encodes visual information remains a fundamental challenge in cognitive neuroscience. Sparse dictionary learning (SDL) has recently been applied to fMRI to discover visual features represented in the visual cortex. Existing approaches, however, depend on a vision-language model to identify the feature at discovery, and report limited discovery of the low-level visual features processed in early retinotopic visual regions that play an essential role in human visual cognition. We propose an automatic framework that systematically discovers visual features encoded in the human visual cortex, encompassing both high-level and low-level visual features. The framework decomposes fMRI responses across the full visual hierarchy with Matryoshka sparse autoencoders applied per region of interest, interprets the resulting fMRI activity patterns with a vision-language model, and introduces a set of feature channels to recover the low-level visual features that language-based interpretation fails to capture. On the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) and on the Brain Encoder Generated Dataset (BEGD), a separate set of synthesized responses from a transformer brain encoder, the low-level stream recovers thousands of interpretable low-level visual features from early retinotopic visual regions, where prior language-based pipelines report limited discovery. The high-level stream recovers interpretable semantic visual features on both datasets and generalizes to BOLD5000. Our analysis further reveals a systematic confound in language-based interpretation: fMRI activity patterns whose true representation is a low-level visual feature can be misidentified as a semantic visual feature when that feature co-varies with a salient semantic visual feature.

articles_hidden.title: Will members of 12-step recovery groups oppose the use of GLP-1 agonists for addiction?
articles_hidden.authors: Wayne Kepner; Steven Klein; Keith Humphreys
articles_hidden.abstract: The integration of pharmacotherapy into abstinence-oriented recovery communities has historically been met with friction. However, a new dynamic may be emerging with the rise of GLP-1 agonists (e.g., semaglutide). While robust clinical trial data for GLP-1s regarding the treatment of substance use disorders remains unclear, these new medications are being adopted off-label by innovators in abstinence-oriented treatment facilities and selectively within the 12-step recovery community. This commentary provides an analysis of this phenomenon through the application of Rogers’ Diffusion of Innovations theory. We argue that unlike previous medications which faced medication stigma for their psychoactive properties, it may be possible that GLP-1s are being met with less resistance from the recovery community because their mechanism of action is culturally congruent with the 12-step goal of relieving the mental obsession of addiction. We posit that this new phenomenon represents a practice-based evidence signal that deserves attention; perhaps the 12-step recovery community is not as anti-medication as once thought.

articles_hidden.title: Brief Exposure Therapy With Exercise For PTSD: A Pilot Study Using Single Case Experimental Design
articles_hidden.authors: Troy Hubert; Shannon Sauer-Zavala; Josh Cisler; Gopalkumar Rakesh; Thomas Adams
articles_hidden.abstract: Background: Trauma-focused exposure therapies are highly effective treatments for posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), but important limitations exist. Animal and human research collectively indicate that aerobic exercise can improve the consolidation of fear-extinction memories, suggesting exercise could enhance therapeutic exposure. Methods: The current study is an open-label pilot clinical trial using a community sample (n=6) of adults with PTSD to evaluate the acceptability, feasibility, and efficacy of an eight-session brief exposure therapy (BET) and aerobic exercise treatment for PTSD. The acceptability and feasibility were examined through participants’ perceptions of treatment, engagement with treatment, and therapists' adherence to the treatment protocol. We used a staggered baseline single-case experimental design (SCED), with visual and quantitative analyses, to evaluate the intervention's preliminary effects on PTSD symptom severity. Results: The BET and exercise protocol was rated as an acceptable treatment that led to greater improvements than they originally expected. During treatment, only one session was late canceled (2% of all sessions), zero sessions had no-shows, and zero participants dropped out of treatment. Visual Analysis indicated a significant effect of the BET and exercise treatment on PTSD symptom severity from baseline to treatment and follow-up phases. Conclusion: Findings indicate that eight sessions of brief imaginal exposure combined with exercise is an acceptable and feasible treatment that has the potential to quickly and significantly reduce PTSD symptoms. These data add to a growing body of literature indicating exposure and exercise treatments have great promise. Future research should evaluate augmenting safety learning with exercise in well-powered, double-blind clinical trials.

articles_hidden.title: Development and psychometric properties of the CDI-IIIR for language assessment of 30- to 48-month-olds
articles_hidden.authors: Philip Dale; Adriana Weisleder; Alexandra Carstensen; Sefela Londiwe Yalala; George Kachergis; Virginia A. Marchman
articles_hidden.abstract: The Macarthur-Bates Communicative Development Inventories (CDI) are a set of widely used parent-report instruments for measuring young children’s language development. The most widely used measures for English-speaking children are the CDIs for 8-30 months. There is a strong need for both clinical and research purpose for comparable measures for three-year-olds. The previously published U.S. English CDI-III yielded norms for 30-37 months only, due to ceiling effects, and assessed limited aspects of language. Recent adaptations for Swedish and other Scandinavian languages, have used a different design and showed strong psychometric properties for children 2.5-4 years old. The current study utilizes insights from that work to revise the CDI-III for an expanded target age range, and to incorporate more aspects of language, including morphology and metalinguistic and print awareness. Results are presented for a sample of 202 children as reported on a pilot version of the new instrument, for both the full set of items and those items selected on the basis of IRT analysis for the final instrument, and also for a preliminary norming sample of 322 children utilizing the final instrument. The CDI-IIIR appears to have good reliability and developmental sensitivity across the target age range of 30 through 48 months. A larger norming sample, and validation evidence, are essential next steps.

articles_hidden.title: GPT-4 reasons like infants about objects but not agents
articles_hidden.authors: Alyson Wong; Bill Thompson; Fei Xu
articles_hidden.abstract: Theory of Mind (ToM) is central to human social cognition and is critical for successfully navigating the social world. However, most work to date has explored explicit ToM in AI, particularly with large language models (LLMs), and has found mixed results. In contrast, decades of developmental psychology research with human infants has found remarkable, early-emerging implicit ToM. However, little work has explored implicit ToM in LLMs. The current study investigates implicit social reasoning abilities in GPT-4 using model-facing versions of classic infant experiments. In Experiment 1, we explored GPT-4’s implicit ToM abilities across four social reasoning tasks adapted from infant paradigms. In Experiment 2, we explored whether GPT-4 was capable of physical reasoning to contrast with social reasoning in Experiments 1 and 2. Across these three experiments, our results suggest that there may be domain differences in GPT-4’s reasoning abilities, such that GPT-4 struggled with social reasoning tasks despite performing very well on physical reasoning tasks. These findings highlight the importance of systematic exploration of social reasoning in LLMs and provide insight into potential deficits in GPT-4’s social reasoning abilities.

articles_hidden.title: Developmental Trajectories of Maths Ability and Socio-Emotional Health in Children with and without Hearing Difficulties
articles_hidden.authors: Andrea Salins; Serje Robidoux; Carola Ruiz Hornblas; Dung Tran; Rebecca Bull
articles_hidden.abstract: Hearing difficulties (HD) in childhood can be associated with emotional and behavioural difficulties (EBD, including attention, peer relations, internalising symptoms, anxiety and externalising symptoms) and can have diverse impacts on educational outcomes, including mathematics. This study has two aims: firstly, to analyse if children with HD differ from typically developing children (TD) in maths and EBD and secondly, to examine the longitudinal bidirectional relationships between maths and EBD in children with HD and TD children. The analyses, t-test and structural equation modelling, are applied on the data of children from 5 to 11 years of age from four large longitudinal datasets from Australia (n = 2,340), the United Kingdom (n = 5,254) and two from the United States (n = 1,537 and 6,343). The findings indicate that children with HD present with weaker maths performance, and more symptoms of EBD than TD children (Aim 1). As for the second aim, the findings regarding the relationships between EBD at age 5 and maths at age 7/8 are inconsistent. Attentional difficulties were consistently predictive of lower maths performance in both HD and TD children, whereas externalising symptoms were consistently unrelated to maths performance. However, findings regarding peer relations are inconsistent for both groups of children, while higher internalising symptoms were consistently related to poorer maths only for TD children, and higher anxiety related to weaker maths performance only for HD children. In contrast, lower performance in maths at age 7/8 was consistently related to a higher presence of EBD symptoms at age 11 for both groups.

articles_hidden.title: A Source-Specific Approach to Internalised Sexual Prejudice: Scale Development and Initial Validation
articles_hidden.authors: Joel Anderson; Natalie Amos; Michael Thai; Jordan Daniel Xavier Hinton
articles_hidden.abstract: Internalised sexual prejudice (ISP) is theorised as the incorporation of social devaluation into negative evaluations of one’s own sexuality. Existing measures, however, generally assess these evaluations without distinguishing the social sources associated with them. We developed the Source-Specific Internalised Sexual Prejudice Scale (SS-ISP), a dual-dimensional 12-item measure assessing negative feelings about one’s own sexuality in response to prejudice from straight people or from other LGBTQA+ people with the same six items presented for each source. Across four studies, we examined its content, structure, invariance across groups, initial validity, and temporal stability. In Study 1, relevance ratings from content experts (n = 15 social psychology researchers) supported retaining six of the eight candidate items under both source frames. Exploratory factor analysis in Study 2 (n = 276 gay men) identified two related source-specific factors. Study 3 replicated this structure in an independent sample (n = 982 LGBTQA+ adults), and supported scalar invariance across cisgender gay men, lesbian women, bisexual men, and bisexual women. Both dimensions demonstrated high internal consistency and positive associations with an established measure of internalised sexual prejudice and concurrent psychological distress. Group differences emerged for LGBTQA+-source ISP, but not for straight-source ISP. Both source-specific dimensions contributed to explaining concurrent psychological distress beyond conventional ISP. An exploratory comparison indicated a stronger adjusted association for LGBTQA+-source ISP than for straight-source ISP. Study 4 (n = 284) indicated moderate 12-month test–retest reliability (ICCs = .65–.68). The findings support distinguishing source-linked manifestations of ISP and retaining their reported social context within its measurement.

articles_hidden.title: Toward Evidence-Based Human-Centered AI and Human-AI Interaction: A Cross-Domain Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Xinyi Wang; Christine Lo; Wei-Hsiang Lo; Manhua Wang; Gaojian Huang
articles_hidden.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly used to support decision-making, automate tasks, personalize services, and improve system performance across domains such as healthcare, education, transportation, cybersecurity, manufacturing, and workplace productivity. As AI adoption expands, clearer guidance is needed to connect human-centered design principles with measurable human outcomes. This systematic review synthesized 44 empirical studies on human-centered AI (HCAI) and human-AI interaction (HAX) to examine measurement approaches, framework categories, AI roles, and domain-specific findings. The reviewed studies showed that AI support was often associated with improved objective outcomes, including task performance and decision quality. Subjective outcomes, including trust, satisfaction, usability, workload, and perceived control, were more variable and depended on transparency, explanation design, task fit, user expertise, and the level of human control. Across studies, human-led AI support was the most common role, especially in high-stakes domains where humans retained final authority. Collaborative AI appeared in tasks requiring shared activity, feedback, or adaptive support, while AI-led support appeared mainly within mixed-role systems. Domain-specific findings showed that healthcare emphasized accuracy, reliability, and overreliance; education emphasized engagement, scaffolding, and ownership; transportation emphasized safety, timing, modality, and trust calibration; and other domains emphasized fairness, transparency, adoption, and acceptance. This review contributes a cross-domain synthesis that connects HCAI and HAX principles with AI roles, evaluation measures, and human outcomes, supporting future frameworks that are easier to evaluate and apply in real-world settings.

articles_hidden.title: Developmental changes in children’s production of line drawings in global contexts: Evidence from Kisumu, Kenya
articles_hidden.authors: Rebecca Zhu; Joab Ochieng Arieda; Tabitha Nduku; Zachary Watson; Tarun Sepuri; Bria Long; Judith Fan; Michael C. Frank
articles_hidden.abstract: Children growing up in environments with many drawing opportunities improve dramatically at producing recognizable drawings over the course of childhood. Does this same developmental trajectory hold for children growing up in environments with fewer drawing opportunities? We measured children’s ability to produce recognizable drawings in a context where children have relatively fewer drawing opportunities and experiences with visual media, specifically Kisumu, Kenya. By leveraging within-context variation in children’s drawing experience, we estimated the strength of the association between how often a child draws and how recognizable their drawings are. A preregistered sample of 120 4- to 9-year-olds drew 12 object categories in random order. Children produced more recognizable drawings with age, even after controlling for their tracing abilities. Moreover, younger children with more drawing experience produced more recognizable drawings, even after controlling for tracing ability and other home environment variables. These results suggest commonalities in drawing development across cultures and document the experience-dependence of drawing development in global contexts.

articles_hidden.title: Mental Load and the Limits of Time-Based Work–Life Balance Policy
articles_hidden.authors: Iara Teixeira; Henrique Pereira
articles_hidden.abstract: Work–life balance policies can redistribute time without transferring responsibility for anticipating and coordinating care. This conceptual article asks when changes in time and task allocation permit caregivers to stop monitoring care needs. Integrating research on cognitive household labor, work–family resources, psychological recovery, and social care, it develops a model linking responsibility, authority, and the opportunity to disengage. The model proposes that continued answerability sustains monitoring and anticipatory vigilance even when another person performs the associated tasks. A dependable successor, understood as a person or institution able to assume responsibility for a defined care need, is proposed as one relational condition supporting disengagement. Gender, socioeconomic conditions, family composition, institutional recognition, and workplace arrangements shape access to this condition. The contribution is to specify how responsibility is retained or transferred within broader accounts of demands and resources, rather than to treat those accounts as exclusively concerned with time. Testable propositions distinguish changes in task performance from changes in monitoring, identify boundary conditions, and guide research across care arrangements. Using European work–life balance provisions as an illustrative policy context, the article proposes indicators for evaluating whether leave, flexibility, and services redistribute cognitive responsibility and support recovery, alongside their effects on participation in employment.

articles_hidden.title: Interoceptive Processing in Boredom Proneness: Sensing Without Making Sense
articles_hidden.authors: Chantal Trudel; James Danckert
articles_hidden.abstract:
Boredom proneness has been linked to a disrupted relationship with one's internal states, yet the
mechanism underlying this disruption remains unclear. One possibility is that this disruption
reflects a difficulty in translating interoceptive signals into meaningful predictions about internal
states, rather than a basic failure to detect them. Across two studies, we examined whether this
disrupted relationship reflects interpretive challenges, a deficit in cardiac interoceptive accuracy,
or both. Study 1 (N = 124) was a direct replication confirming that highly boredom prone
individuals report attending intensely to bodily sensations while struggling to interpret them — a
pattern that held across a combined sample of 350 adults and yielded moderate-to-strong
correlations with established measures of self-focused attention and interoceptive sensory
confusion. Study 2 (N = 121) administered a heartbeat counting task to determine whether this
disrupted relationship was due to deficient interoceptive processing or interpretive failure.
Boredom proneness was unrelated to objective heartbeat counting accuracy but remained
associated with self-reported interoceptive sensory confusion. Converging with Study 1, this
pattern suggests that boredom proneness is best characterized by a difficulty in interpreting internal
signals than by a basic interoceptive perceptual deficit. Together, these findings are consistent with
predictive processing accounts of boredom proneness where those high in trait boredom struggle
to generate meaningful predictions from interoceptive cues. Whether this dissociation between
self-reported and objective cardiac interoception generalizes across different measurement
approaches and populations remains an open question that future work could examine using more
sensitive interoceptive tasks and trial-level prediction error metrics.

articles_hidden.title: Adaptation reduces perceptual effects of inter-observer metamerism with narrow-band primaries
articles_hidden.authors: Takuma Morimoto; Allie C. Schneider; Hannah Smithston
articles_hidden.abstract: Narrow-band display primaries increase observer metamerism, but to what extent does chromatic adaptation mitigate the perceptual consequences of these effects? We simulated 10,000 individualized observers viewing real-world reflectances under varied illuminants and optimized a virtual RGB display to reproduce each observer’s cone excitations. Between-observer disagreement was quantified using ΔE′ in CAM16-UCS. Without adaptation, metamerism increased as primaries narrowed, reaching a median ΔE′ of 4.8. Increasing adaptation reduced metamerism monotonically: complete adaptation reduced observers’ ΔE′ by a median of 40–67%, with the largest proportional reduction for the narrowest primaries. Adaptation to shared stimuli may therefore align visual experiences across individuals.

articles_hidden.title: Trait or Bias? Why item keying is indispensable when comparing language model responses across languages
articles_hidden.authors: Qing Li
articles_hidden.abstract: Cross-linguistic differences in large language model (LLM) questionnaire responses are increasingly interpreted as evidence of culturally patterned behaviour. Such inferences, however, assume that observed score differences reflect variation in the target construct rather than artefacts of measurement. The present study examines this assumption using three established Likert measures of social orientation administered in English and Chinese to four contemporary LLMs. Leveraging balanced-keying scales, we decompose observed cross-linguistic differences into a trait-related component and a response-bias component associated with item keying. We further test the role of item wording through keying manipulations that preserve substantive content while altering item direction. Across models and instruments, the observed language effect was found to comprise two separable components of comparable magnitude but opposite sign. The bias component was highly consistent, with English prompting producing greater agreement tendencies than Chinese prompting in every balanced-keying condition. Rewording experiments showed that the effect tracked item wording rather than substantive content, while analyses of forward-keyed instruments indicated that the two components were confounded in conventional scores. As a consequence, identical composite scores could arise from different combinations of trait-related variation and response bias. These findings do not challenge the existence of cross-linguistic variation in LLM responses. Rather, they challenge the interpretation of observed score differences as direct indicators of underlying cultural orientation. The results suggest that cross-linguistic differences in questionnaire responses reflect both construct-related variation and language-dependent response tendencies, and that balanced-keying designs are necessary to distinguish between them. More broadly, the study highlights the importance of measurement validity in cross-linguistic evaluations of LLMs and argues that prompt language should be treated as a substantive measurement variable rather than a neutral medium of expression.

articles_hidden.title: Neurospirituality Reappraised: Brain Mechanisms of Transcendent Experience and Beyond
articles_hidden.authors: Marleide da Mota Gomes
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background:
Subjective experiences featuring altered self-awareness, temporal perception, or spatial boundaries—termed Non-Ordinary Experiences (NOEs)—occur across clinical neurology, psychiatry, and psychedelic medicine, including in insular ecstatic seizures, meditation, breathwork, hypnosis, and psychedelic therapy. 
Objective:
To synthesize neurobiological and clinical literature on NOEs for neurologists by presenting three heuristic frameworks: 
1.	A six-dimension phenomenological taxonomy; 
2.	A tri-level descriptive taxonomy (computational "software", neuromodulatory-autonomic "firmware", and network "hardware"); 
3.	The Trigger–Dynamic Psyche–4E Appraisal–Outcome Model, which maps how acute neurodynamic shifts resolve into adaptive growth or clinical distress without reducing existential meaning to neural activity. 
Methods:
Narrative synthesis of systematic reviews, coordinate-based meta-analyses, and key theoretical frameworks sourced via PubMed/MEDLINE. 
Results:
Conflating spirituality, religion, and NOEs causes construct contamination in neuroimaging, compounded by unvalidated single-item measures and non-independent cohorts. An fMRI meta-analysis of meditation (34 studies, N=700) reveals aggregate recruitment of the right rolandic operculum, left insula, supplementary motor area, and hippocampus, arguing against a singular "spiritual center". First-person reports are mapped using a six-dimension schema (experiential content, temporal dynamics, spatial dynamics, volitional dynamics/agency, ownership/embodiment, cognitive stance). Mechanistically, states are organized across three bidirectionally coupled levels: computational inference ("software"), neuromodulatory-autonomic state-setting ("firmware"), and large-scale networks ("hardware"). Five entry routes (meditation, psychedelics, breathwork, hypnosis, focal neurological events) are hypothesized to share shifts in Bayesian precision weighting and network decoupling within the master Trigger–Dynamic Psyche–4E Appraisal–Outcome Model. Crucially, long-term outcomes (integration vs. distress) are not dictated by acute brain states alone, but are mediated by contextual filtering through the 4E Appraisal Prism (embodied, embedded, enacted, extended dimensions). 
Conclusions:
Neurospirituality bridges network neuroscience, clinical neurology, and person-centered care. Clarifying biological substrates does not resolve existential validity. Clinicians must maintain a strict distinction between biological mechanisms, subjective experiences, and personal meanings (the Epistemological Invariant) to avoid pathologizing adaptive states or romanticizing neurological disease. 
Key terms: Spirituality; Neuroimaging; Meditation; Hallucinogens; Epilepsy.

articles_hidden.title: Incentivizing Open Science: Examining the Open Data Citation Advantage in Visual Search Research
articles_hidden.authors: Jonathan Nir
articles_hidden.abstract:
In the wake of psychology’s credibility revolution, open science practices such as data sharing have become more prevalent, yet researchers often cite a lack of professional incentives as a barrier to adoption. This report examines the association between data sharing and scholarly impact in visual search and eye-movement literature, building on the systematic audit by Godwin et al. (2025).
I extended their dataset with bibliometric metadata from the OpenAlex registry and compared field-normalized, accumulated, and time-resolved citation impact between articles that did and did not share data. Although articles that shared data showed a small citation advantage in unadjusted analyses, this difference was no longer statistically significant after adjusting for publication characteristics such as publication age and journal citedness. A time-resolved analysis revealed a small association between sharing status and the trajectory of citation accrual, but did not establish a robust early citation advantage. Citation impact also did not differ by data granularity: sharing fine-grained fixation-level data did not confer greater benefit than sharing coarser participant-level summaries.
These observational findings provide no robust evidence of an overall citation advantage associated with data sharing in this research domain, nor of an additional advantage for finer-grained data.  They do not establish that data sharing has no citation benefit, but highlight the importance of examining how its association with scholarly impact varies across research contexts and over time.

articles_hidden.title: Revisiting Tau indices for single-case data analysis: Potential limitations and proposed alternatives
articles_hidden.authors: Rumen Manolov; Antonio Solanas
articles_hidden.abstract: There are many different data analytical procedures applicable to data obtained via single-case experimental designs, with mean differences, regression-based procedures, and nonoverlap indices being among the most frequently used ones. The possibilities are reduced when the data are ordinal and/or variable and cannot be meaningfully summarized by straight lines. For such scenarios, nonoverlap indices become prominent. The current text is a continuation of previous discussions related to the quantification of trend in the context of using nonoverlap indices. Focusing on the Tau indices by Parker and colleagues and by Tarlow, we underline potential drawbacks that have not been discussed previously, while also suggesting alternatives. Specifically, we point at situations in which underestimation and overestimation of trend are possible, as well as discussing the quantification problems arising in case trend levels off by reaching an upper or lower bound. The aim of the review of existing options and of the tentatively proposed alternatives is to ignite further discussion regarding how to deal with trend without assuming that a straight line (or any specific nonlinear model) is a good representation of the data.
